title: If you bought an iPhone Duo, have you kept or returned it? [Poll]
snippet: When Apple announced the iPhone Duo back in September, the company called it “the most transformational change to iPhone since the original,” and there’s no doubt that it generated a huge amount of excitement. But a new report suggests that for some buyers the novelty quickly wore off, and they ended up returning their devices. Is this just a handful of people, or is it more common … ? more…
fullText:
When Apple announced the iPhone Duo back in September, the company called it “the most transformational change to iPhone since the original,” and there’s no doubt that it generated a huge amount of excitement.

But a new report suggests that for some buyers the novelty quickly wore off, and they ended up returning their devices. Is this just a handful of people, or is it more common … ?

It’s been a very long time since any smartphone launch has generated quite so much buzz. Apple called it a breakthrough in iPhone design.

iPhone Duo features a breakthrough foldable design that’s beautiful, versatile, and durable, opening up possibilities that feel entirely new yet remarkably familiar […] 

“iPhone Duo is the most transformational change to iPhone since the original. With an entirely new design and intuitive experiences, it shows what’s possible when hardware and software are engineered together and redefines what it means to use a foldable phone,” said John Ternus.

Despite not really being the target market for the phone, I was still wowed by the launch video and remained incredibly impressed when I got some hands-on time with one.

Many couldn’t resist buying one despite the price – but The Verge notes that not everyone has ending up keeping the device. Apple allows you to return any product within 14 days for a full refund without having to give any reason. That window has come to an end for some of the first buyers and the site’s Alison Johnson spoke with some of those who’d decided to take advantage of it.

	

There were a few specific issues:

It’s too heavy and bulky

The outer screen is too small

The cameras aren’t as good as those on the iPhone 18 Pro

But the more fundamental reason for some is that it hasn’t really lived up to their hopes for a multifunctional device.

“If I can have an iPad in my pocket, that would be great.” So thought Ben Seligson, a content creator, photographer, and now former iPhone Duo owner […] “Usually I’d throw a YouTube video on the iPad or throw a podcast up. And then I start cooking dinner and leave my iPad in one spot, but I’d have my phone in my pocket if I got a text, or I needed to set a timer or something like that.” With the Duo, the phone was also the iPad on the counter, so a quick reply became much more of an interruption.

I’m curious as to whether this is just a small minority of buyers or a more common phenomenon. If you bought a Duo early enough to have hit the end of the return window, please take our poll to let us know whether you decided to keep it or return it – and do share your reasons in the comments (which are now back).

Oh, and the good news for anyone buying one now is that you’ll have a lot longer to make up your mind, with the extended return window for the holidays in place. You can now return anything bought today through January 8.

title: Databricks’ new AI agent tells CEO Ali Ghodsi the unvarnished truth
snippet: At 12,000 employees, AI Ghodsi is the first to admit that he can't know everyone and that they are unlikely to confess the things that go wrong to him. But he doesn't need them to. He uses Databricks' newly revised Genie agent for that.
fullText:
Databricks on Wednesday unveiled an updated version of its AI agent Genie, which can now perform multi-step jobs that take extended work to finish.  It does this through an ontology that Databricks built to give Genie the context it needs from the information that customers store on the Databricks platform.

Corporate leaders can now assign the agent a wide range of tasks, and it will complete them unsupervised, the company says. To prove the point, Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi showed me how he uses it internally. Instead of a product demo, he fired up his actual agent and walked me through his most recent chats and charts.

He showed me how it analyzed the parts of an employee satisfaction survey where the company didn’t score well, and how it helped him rate (and discard) fixes for those low scores that some executives suggested. He showed me how it summarized a big sales pitch to a prospect that went poorly — including the features the prospect said it needed before buying.

It also prepped him for a podcast interview by reviewing his previous appearances and developing likely questions. While we talked, he even had it tell him what he should say to me. (And its advice on that wasn’t bad.)

The fascinating part was that Ghodsi was using Genie to find the stuff that he’s now unlikely to hear as the big boss. It was a source of unvarnished truth about what wasn’t going well that he needed to address.

“Have you heard of Dunbar’s number? The magic number is 150,” he said when I pointed this out. Named for British anthropologist Robin Dunbar, it’s theoretically the maximum number of people with whom humans can maintain stable relationships. In a small startup, a CEO knows everyone, has direct relationships with them, and they feel safe to tell him negative info straight up.

With 12,000 employees, Ghodsi is the first to admit he can’t know everyone. At that size, a salesperson isn’t likely to confess a disastrous sales call to the CEO. An HR manager isn’t likely to confess that their idea for increasing employee satisfaction will probably fail.

“Anyone who has more than 150 employees, which is a lot of companies, a lot of people can get value out of this,” he said of AI agents generally and his product, Genie, specifically.

Ghodsi’s own use of Genie (often called dogfooding, from the phrase “eating your own dogfood”) is one reason why Databricks is now pitching it as an always-on agent for business leaders. He says he also uses it in his personal life, rather than a security-questionable alternative like OpenClaw or Instinct or Muse.

He believes Genie can do for the business side what AI, agents and harnesses (the software that wraps around an AI model and lets it use tools) are doing for programmers. As for the risk that agents will ratchet up corporate AI costs, Ghodsi has an answer for that, too. He said costs can be controlled through Databricks’ Unity Gateway product. It allows companies to set usage limits and to swap in less expensive open-weight models.

title: OpenAI acquires Odessia, travel startup created by Sonder founder
snippet: OpenAI has not yet said what its plans are for the future of travel. But Sonder founder Francis Davidson is a well-known figure in the travel industry.
fullText:
OpenAI has acquired an AI travel agent called Odessia, according to Odessia’s founder, Francis Davidson. Davidson says in a post announcing the deal that he’s now working for OpenAI, helping the AI lab with the future of travel.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but this looks like an acqui-hire. Davidson’s announcement focused largely on how he built his AI travel agent Odessia by directing teams of AI agents. The year-old Odessia raised a $6 million pre-seed round led by Sequoia and launched its AI travel agent around five months ago. Davidson says that it had helped early adopters plan millions of dollars’ worth of travel, but the tool has already been shut down.

An OpenAI spokesperson confirmed the hire to TechCrunch. “We’re thrilled to welcome Francis to OpenAI. Francis is a proven founder who has built multiple businesses to help people travel, and we’re excited he’s chosen to build with us.”

However the AI lab has not announced new travel-specific products or plans. It does, however, count such companies as Bookings.com, Expedia, and KAYAK as customers or partners. Travel is also one of the main areas that people are using personal AI assistants to help with. And, back in July 2025, when OpenAI launched its ChatGPT agent, it mentioned travel as one of its potential uses. 

OpenAI’s spokesperson didn’t have more to share on its plans for travel-related products, except to say that travel is one of the areas that chatbot users frequently ask about. “1.2 billion people turn to ChatGPT each week for help with everyday tasks — from understanding their health, figuring out what to make for dinner, building a budget, and even planning a trip. We see a real opportunity to make these experiences even more useful,” the spokesperson said.  

Acquiring Odessia is interesting for another reason. Davidson is well known in the travel industry after he founded a travel startup called Sonder as a college student in 2014. It was sort of like Airbnb, but it focused on short-term leasing of upscale apartments in major cities worldwide. The pandemic badly hurt it, and as it climbed out of that rut, it went public via a SPAC but didn’t raise as much money as it needed, Davidson later said in a post announcing his resignation as CEO in June 2025.

When a key partnership with Marriott fell through, the company went into bankruptcy and wound down. The bankruptcy trustee sold Sonder’s name, trademarks, and website domain in 2026 to TravelAI, and that website operates as a curated guide to the kind of travel rental properties that Sonder was once known for. Prior to its downfall, Davidson had built Sonder into a unicorn with $143 million in revenues. While Sonder was not, ultimately, a success story, Davidson is the kind of battle-scarred founder that Silicon Valley often values.

So we’ll have to wait and see what OpenAI has in store now with travel, now that he’s joined the company.

title: Google DeepMind analysis proves Signal and WhatsApp encryption is secure
snippet: The Signal protocol has long been considered the gold standard for end-to-end encrypted messaging, with Edward Snowden a notable advocate. Now a Google DeepMind analysis has “formally verified” the security of the protocol. In addition to its use in the Signal app, the same protocol is also used by WhatsApp and Google Messages, and the work has been described as “a landmark development” … more…
fullText:
The Signal protocol has long been considered the gold standard for end-to-end encrypted messaging, with Edward Snowden a notable advocate. Now a Google DeepMind analysis has “formally verified” the security of the protocol.

In addition to its use in the Signal app, the same protocol is also used by WhatsApp and Google Messages, and the work has been described as “a landmark development” … 

“Formal verification” is the term given to mathematically proving or disproving that a cryptographic algorithm or protocol satisfies its security claims under all conditions. It guarantees that there is no situation in which the protocol will fail. This is a far higher standard than traditional testing methods which seek to find vulnerabilities but cannot promise that others do not exist.

Using agentic AI to carry out formal verification is a huge breakthrough for cryptography and AI alike. It is, however, extremely computationally demanding, so Google told Wired it’s unclear as yet how practical it will be to use it more broadly.

DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process. “We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

It’s important to note that the validation is for the protocol itself rather than the Signal app as a whole. However, encouragement can be taken from the fact that when tested against older versions of Signal that contained known vulnerabilities, it identified those and flagged them as failing formal verification.

Also worth stating is that Google was able to build on some past formal verification work already completed without the use of AI. This analysis took four weeks, and the scale of resources required has not yet been disclosed, so we shouldn’t expect a whole array of other protocols to be validated overnight. All the same, this is a very big deal.

fullText:
It’s tempting to seek out the do-everything wireless gaming headset with noise cancellation, phenomenal sound quality, multiplatform connectivity, swappable batteries — you name it. But if you just want the basics done well, Sony’s new $99.99 PlayStation Pulse headset is worth considering. It has very good sound and just enough extras, even if you use more gadgets than just your PlayStation 5.

Inside the Pulse’s nondescript ear cup shells are custom planar magnetic drivers, which deliver clean, detailed sound whether you’re gaming, listening to music, or both. They aren’t bass-heavy or too shrill; their default equalizer is pleasing and punchy, though you can also tweak it in the PS5’s interface, like other Pulse headsets. They’re not Sony’s first audio gaming product to feature this type of high-end driver (the first was in 2023), but they are the most affordable at $99.

$99

The Pulse comes with either a white or black headband, with a soft-touch underside and a decent amount of give near the top of your head where it rests its weight. Thankfully, the headset is lightweight and offers size adjustments that go beyond what my large head requires for comfort. These are some of the only headphones I’ve used with ear cups that can rotate 180 degrees in either direction.

Functionally, the Pulse stands out as a semi-affordable wireless headset that can stream audio from PlayStation Link (Sony’s low-latency, lossless wireless connection) and Bluetooth simultaneously. It includes a USB-C Link dongle that lets you pair it quickly with whatever you plug it into, whether it’s a PS5, PC, or Nintendo Switch 2.

The headset’s ear cup controls include a dedicated Bluetooth button that, beyond pairing with another gadget, lets you pause or resume Bluetooth content (it can also answer or hang up calls). You can also control Bluetooth audio volume using the integrated volume rocker, but only when a device isn’t connected via PlayStation Link. In simultaneous audio mode, the rocker adjusts audio solely for the device connected via the Link dongle.

If you have Sony’s PlayStation Portal, the Pulse can connect directly to the handheld without the Link dongle, just as Sony’s Pulse Elite and Explore can. It’s so convenient, and I hope Sony pushes for more devices that integrate the Link wireless technology in the future.

The Pulse isn’t the only headset that Sony has in the works. Its Pulse Edge wireless headset doesn’t have an exact launch date or price, but the company touts that it packs in twice as many magnets in its drivers (eight versus four), active noise cancellation, and a detachable boom mic that will likely provide better-sounding voice audio than the built-in mic in the standard Pulse. It will also include game / chat audio controls, a 3.5mm jack, and a carrying case.

While the $99 Pulse is comparatively light on features, Sony’s focus on providing standout audio quality and comfort makes it worth seeking out if you have a PS5 and are on a strict budget for your next wireless headset.

title: Adobe Is Giving Its AI Agents Even More to Do
snippet: Across Firefly and Creative Cloud, apps are getting even deeper into creative work.
fullText:
Would you use an always-on AI agent such as Claude Duet or OpenAI’s Dot to edit your photos? At Adobe Max on Tuesday, the company announced it’s expanding its local MCP integrations with more third-party companies to enable more autonomous creative work.

MCP, or Model Context Protocol, is an open-source protocol for connecting AI systems to external apps and databases. AI agents and MCPs act as a two-way street. Agents, or fancy bots, can complete tasks independently.

For example, if you wanted your OpenAI agents (or Dots, whatever you call them) to edit a project in Photoshop, the MCP pathway would allow ChatGPT to run agents to edit the design in the Photoshop beta desktop app — no need to search through the toolbar if you’re not familiar with it.

			

More from CNET

The new MCP integrations are in preview now. The idea is to give people more choice by letting them use their preferred AI app to help them work in select Creative Cloud apps.

Over the past year, Adobe has been working with AI companies to bring its creative knowledge and tech to ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot as Adobe plugins. It’s also brought external models from AI companies into Firefly, Adobe’s AI hub. Now, Adobe is deepening its relationships with third-party AI vendors to adapt to the agentic AI era.

Bringing your own agents offers a degree of user control, according to Shilpa Anand, vice president of global strategic partnerships. “These new models allow me to actually do things faster, experience the full power of the application and really make it more accessible to a broader set of users who are not experts in our workflow,” Anand told me.

Adobe’s agentic AI journey

Agentic AI has been a huge focus for tech companies this year. It’s the next step for companies that want to move beyond mere chat and information-gathering AI capabilities. 

Adobe has been driving toward this vision for a while. It released AI assistants in Photoshop and Adobe Express that set the foundation for June’s official launch of Adobe creative agents.

But AI agents from frontier labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic caused trouble this summer when they escaped testing environments and hacked real websites. Anand told me that safety and security are “table stakes” for Adobe and that there haven’t been any issues aligning with other AI companies on safety precautions.

When considering partnerships, the company also considers which AI models will be most useful for Adobe’s creative customers, which is why Firefly includes models from big players including Google, as well as more specialized AI companies, such as ElevenLabs for AI audio tech. (Adobe acquired Topaz Labs, which makes AI photo editing software, earlier this year.)

Those creative AI agents are getting new capabilities across Creative Cloud apps, too. In Firefly, the company’s AI hub, its AI assistant should now be better at multistep or more complex tasks, and it has a new “plan mode” in preview that lets you review the agent’s plan before it starts running.

New “always-on” Firefly AI agents do exactly what the name implies: They’re always working and can handle predefined tasks, such as assessing image quality in new asset uploads. They’re in preview now, too. And across Illustrator, InDesign, Premiere, After Effects and Frame.io, those AI assistants are getting upgraded capabilities as well.

Adobe is also expanding its partnerships. Microsoft Photos will have a built-in Adobe Express integration, and Microsoft’s Arm-based Windows PCs are getting “optimized” Adobe apps. Disney is also deepening its relationship with Adobe, bringing Adobe’s Firefly AI tech to its creative teams.

Partnerships with AI companies and the integration of agentic capabilities will continue to be a focus for Adobe next year, Anand told me. “Agentic software is really going to enable us to reach more users and empower everyone to create, which is our mission.”

title: Reddit’s New AI-Powered Reviews Are Already Controversial
snippet: The platform’s test of automated product review summaries is sparking concern that advertising will replace human advice.
fullText:
Reddit announced on Tuesday that it’s testing Reviews, an AI-powered shopping feature that aggregates user comments into product summaries, commerce links, and pros-and-cons breakdowns. In a blog post, the company said it wants to organically use discussions on the platform, from conversations about skin care treatments or coffee to headphones, to help people “understand what a product is really like and feel confident deciding whether it’s right for them.”

The Reviews feature promises to make product research easier on a site that’s increasingly focused on shopping recommendations. But the announcement immediately rankled some Reddit users who are concerned it will degrade authentic human-to-human discussion and advice. Many Reddit moderators, or “mods,” tasked with keeping order of communities called subreddits, believe it’ll be hard to distinguish real opinions from straight-up advertising.

According to Reddit, the upcoming feature will surface product reviews in search results and through highlighted product mentions in comment threads, regardless of a group’s rules preventing the promotion of products by users or brands.

			

More from CNET

The test launch of Reviews, which was previewed in February and focused on electronics, will start with about 10,000 products across electronics, health and beauty, home and garden, and fashion and apparel. If the experiment works, Reddit plans to expand the feature outside the US and also increase the range of categories and products.

Mods push back

In a Reddit community for the moderators who enforce platform and subreddit rules, the new AI-powered shopping feature was greeted with skepticism and criticism. Writing in modnews, ProudnotLoud dubbed early tests “an ad-ridden, distracting mess” that made reading threads nearly impossible. 

For moderators who work to keep commercial spam out of their subreddits, the feature poses an existential threat. User nerdshark warned that communities are already being actively targeted by stealth corporate campaigns, arguing that forcing Reviews into these spaces “does vulnerable communities a huge disservice,” especially without an opt-out mechanism.

Some Reddit admins have pushed back against the backlash, clarifying that the embedded product links are search shortcuts rather than paid placements. Yet users remain unconvinced. As CouncilofStrongs countered: “From a user experience, it is an ad.”

Reddit has also recently been testing advertising in search results, which could be a way for brands to reach Reddit users who click a product name even if they aren’t paying for placement in Reddit Reviews.

Automated e-commerce

Given the amount of sites that focus heavily on human-centered reviews (you’re reading one of them), Reddit’s intent to aggregate product information through AI summaries could be seen as another way for traditional media publishers to have their content used without compensation. 

But Reddit maintains the feature is purely informational. In a statement to CNET, a Reddit spokesperson said that Reviews relies exclusively on internal platform content and “does not source, scrape or republish third-party content.” The company said that because each review links to the original discussion, users on the platform “can explore the context and go deeper. “

Reddit also said that brands can’t buy ads to get into Reddit Reviews. “What appears in Reddit Reviews is shaped by Reddit communities, not paid placement,” the spokesperson said. 

However, that reliance on organic Reddit activity brings its own vulnerabilities. One challenge Reddit may face with Reviews is trying to keep its AI focused on authentic human-written reviews versus posts that might come from marketers, coordinated astroturfing or AI-generated spam. Because the platform operates on anonymity, it’s facing an uphill battle with a massive influx of AI bots that could try to game content in Reviews.

The new feature comes alongside Reddit’s recent changes to the platform to detect spam or other manipulated content and keep bots out, including discontinuing support for RSS feeds and limiting access to its content API. The company is also restricting Old Reddit, a previous design version of the platform that has fewer ads. 

A Reddit spokesperson told CNET that the platform has “the least amount of AI slop relative to other[s]” and that it is taking “numerous steps to prevent and enforce against inauthentic content.” 

But while Reddit insists that Reviews will be centered on personal experience and uncorrupted by advertising dollars, many are worried the feature could blur the line between community research and automated e-commerce.

title: Want Apple Intelligence for Your Home Security Camera? You’ll Need These 4 Things
snippet: Apple Intelligence offers smart AI features for compatible cameras, but you’ll need to play by Apple’s rules. Here’s all the requirements.
fullText:
Aqara is one of the few camera brands that works well with Apple products.Aqara

In the past months Apple has unveiled a host of new Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features, with more on the way. And some features immediately caught my attention because they can enable security cameras on Apple devices in all-new ways. The most interesting option even adds video descriptions, essentially using AI to “read” your security clips and give you texts about what’s happening in them, so you don’t have to view them yourself.

It’s a nifty trick, one that I’ve seen come to Google Nest, Arlo, Ring, Blink and other home security camera companies in the past year or two. Now it’s Apple’s turn, but enabling this AI feature takes more work this time around. Apple wants to keep users inside its ecosystem, so there are more requirements than usual for smart video descriptions and similar capabilities. Let’s go through exactly what you’ll need.

1. A newer iPhone or iPad, updated to the latest software

The iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo both can run Apple Intelligence features.Patrick Holland/CNET

Apple Intelligence doesn’t run on just any device. Your first requirement is an iPhone or iPad that can handle it. If you recently downloaded iOS 27 or iPadOS 27 and received an update about Apple Intelligence now being on your device, you should be good to go.

			

More from CNET

Specifically, you’ll need an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max or iPhone 16 model or later to run these features. If you prefer using an iPad, you’ll need the iPad Mini (A17 Pro or later) or an iPad model with the M1 chip or later.

Before you start using security features with Apple Intelligence, make sure everything is updated – you’ll want the latest iOS if you don’t have it yet.

2. A home hub Apple device

The Mini 2 can’t compete with the large HomePod but otherwise does very well. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Smart home devices that work with Apple Home typically need a hub to pair with, and security cameras using Apple Intelligence are no exception. That means you’ll need another Apple device that can act as a hub, and you’ve got several choices.

Apple hubs include the second-gen HomePod, the HomePod Mini and Mini 2 or an Apple TV 4K model. Apple briefly gave some iPads the ability to become home hubs but then stopped, so an iPad won’t be sufficient here.

3. A compatible security camera for Apple Home

Apple’s new camera line has 2.5K resolution and works readily with Apple devices.Ajay Kumar/CNET

You’ll need a security camera that works well with Apple Home, but that’s easier said than done. If you can wait, Apple’s own security camera line, made in partnership with LG, should be here by the end of 2026, and should have the best results.

However, those Apple cams will be very expensive, so I understand if you want to look for a more affordable option. Not many security cams currently work with Apple, but one of the best brands is Aqara, like this Aqara G3650 camera hub ($140) I’m testing right now. Aqara models go down to $40, so there’s plenty of room to save here.

Note that, at least for the base subscription, I’ve seen reports that AI features like video descriptions only work with one camera at a time, so getting a whole fleet of cams won’t make much difference here. And speaking of subscriptions, there’s one final piece you’ll want.

4. The right iCloud Plus subscription

Apple Intelligence features may require an advanced iCloud subscription.

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

You’ll want an iCloud Plus subscription to enable the full suite of Siri AI capabilities and avoid running into daily limits. But to be clear, even if you don’t use Siri AI, these security Apple Intelligence features will require at least a 2TB plan, which starts at $10 per month. That’s not surprising – video descriptions like this typically come with a subscription requirement, up to $20 per month in some cases.

Now you’ve got everything you need for Apple Intelligence security features. To get started, just go to Apple Home, go to Home Settings and make sure Apple Intelligence is toggled on. Then you should be able to choose an added camera to turn on video descriptions.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma

title: Ring’s wheeled and flying robots will patrol your home
snippet: Some people use a whole bunch of fixed cameras to monitor their homes, but Amazon has just announced a more flexible solution through wheeled and flying robots. Both the $250 Drone Cam and $1,000 Rover Cam can respond to alarms or door and window sensor alerts in order to go check out what’s happening and send live video … more…
fullText:
Some people use a whole bunch of fixed cameras to monitor their homes, but Amazon has just announced a more flexible solution through wheeled and flying robots.

Both the $250 Drone Cam and $1,000 Rover Cam can respond to alarms or door and window sensor alerts in order to go check out what’s happening and send live video … 

Amazon says they are the first two Ring Robotics products, with more likely to follow. Both are autonomous.

Ring Drone and Ring Rover are both powered by AI Pilot, a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.

AI Pilot simplifies the customer experience, starting with setup. Simply carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan. It intelligently identifies rooms and suggests patrol points: spots worth extra attention. This could be a side door, windows, a register, or a long corridor, helping eliminate guesswork while also allowing you to add additional points customized to your space and security preferences.

When a patrol or flight is initiated, AI Pilot plans the most efficient route to get to a preset point based on the map it’s created. From there, it reacts in real time—autonomously navigating around furniture, shelving, and any obstacle it encounters.

You can set either device to patrol on a fixed schedule, as well as activate them manually, but they will also automatically respond to sensor alerts and alarms.

When a Ring camera, sensor, or alarm is triggered, [either device] automatically [moves] to previously set patrol points to investigate […] Continuous person motion detection means Ring Rover can alert you and start recording the moment it detects motion in its view—even when docked.

The Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping on December 16 for $999.99, but you can preorder it today. The Drone Cam starts shipping in late January for $249.99, but there’s no preorder yet.

title: Sundrop turns your endless baby photos into recaps, time lapses, and more — without AI
snippet: Sundrop is a new iPhone app that uses Apple's on-device AI to help parents rediscover their favorite photos and create keepsakes without uploading images to the cloud.
fullText:
New parents take a lot of pictures of their children, but those photos often end up languishing in photo galleries, never to be seen again after the initial snap and share.

A new app, Sundrop, aims to make those pictures more useful by turning them into weekly recaps, highlights, time lapses of the child growing up, and other cute scenes, like putting the child’s photo on a magazine cover or a rookie card.

While Google Photos and Apple Photos already provide extensive tools to organize and manage photos, Sundrop is taking aim at a particular niche: parents with a new baby (usually their first!) who take an overwhelming number of photos and want to do more with those pictures.

Image Credits:Sundrop

The app was developed over the past few months by the same team behind the read-it-later app, Matter: Ben Springwater, Sky Lan, and Rob Mackenzie (all dads themselves).

Notably, Sundrop claims it is designed to be private, and processes all photos locally on the device it is installed on. To make this possible, Sundrop taps into Apple’s Vision framework and on-device Core ML (machine learning) models instead of uploading photos to a cloud server or some other hosted AI service.

Both of the child’s parents can use Sundrop together by linking their accounts, which allows the app to sync their shared photos via Apple’s iCloud service. This feature, the company says, means the pictures aren’t sent to any external servers it runs.

Image Credits:Sundrop

In addition, the team notes that no generative AI is used in the creation of its scenes or highlights. 

This differentiates it from many photo-editing apps on the market, including Google’s, which are increasingly tapping generative AI to create new versions of your photos.

Image Credits:Sundrop

To find highlights and recaps, Sundrop scans pictures in the parents’ respective Camera Rolls on their iPhones, skipping things like screenshots or duplicates. It then creates highlights or fun scenes, which it calls “drops.” 

One of these is a recap of the week every Sunday, announced as a Lock Screen notification. Others can put two siblings side-by-side at the same age, generate a time-lapse series of photos or a video of a kid growing up, or cut out a photo of the child and place it into a layered template.

Image Credits:Sundrop

Parents can also manually edit the photos Sundrop uses to make its creations, or use the app to automatically organize the best photos into galleries with other similar shots. 

The app costs $39.99 per year, and offers a week-long free trial. The annual plan also includes Family Sharing, so only one parent needs to purchase it.

fullText:
Instagram launched an Edits app for iPhone back in 2025, with a Mac version introduced just a few days ago. Meta has now supplemented this with an AI-powered Instagram Effect Builder, letting users create imagery for Stories simply by describing what they want to see … 

Instagram Edits is a free video editing app available for both iPhone and Mac. As you’d expect, the latter is the more powerful version, offering a larger workspace, more precise editing controls, and customizable keyboard shortcuts. Notably, the app supports multiple aspect ratios and allows exports as well as uploads, so can be used to produce video for any platform, not just Instagram.

Meta has now launched Instagram Effect Builder to create AI imagery for use in Instagram Stories. While it’s a standalone web-based tool, the company is describing it as an expansion of the Edits app.

One quirk is that any effect you create becomes available to any Instagram user. This usage will, however, link back to your profile.

Today, we’re expanding what you can create with Edits and introducing a new way to share your creativity on Instagram […] With Effect Builder, you don’t need design or coding skills, or prior experience making effects. Describe the look you want, preview it on your own photos, and publish. The effect shows up in Instagram Stories for anyone to use, and whenever someone uses your effect we’ll link back to your profile so that it’s easy for others to find your work.

The web app is currently limited to adult Instagram users in the US.

title: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy
snippet: Leaker Aaron Perris has discovered evidence of a new Mac app in the works at Apple called Harbor, which makes it easy to run local AI models across one or more Macs. more…
fullText:
Leaker Aaron Perris has discovered evidence of a new Mac app in the works at Apple called Harbor, which makes it easy to run local AI models across one or more Macs.

New ‘Harbor’ app revealed at Apple: ‘turns your Mac into a private AI inference server’

The Mac has been getting a lot more popular this year, both because of budget-friendly options like MacBook Neo but also as a tool for running AI models locally on Mac Studio, Mac mini, and more.

It seems Apple plans to lean harder into the latter use case, as leaker Aaron Perris has discovered a new Mac app called Harbor that’s been designed to turn your Mac into a private AI inference server. 

Here’s Perris’s post on X with the details:

Apple is working on a new app called Harbor

Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool… pic.twitter.com/UYJBQeX4Nf

— Aaron (@aaronp613) November 10, 2026

As the post notes, here’s what the app does:

Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency that a single computer can handle alone.

And here are the feature highlights:

Setup in minutes, not hours: “Harbor automatically detects your devices over Thunderbolt 5 to form a cluster. Plug in, start, and you’re running—no manual configuration, no command line, no infrastructure expertise required.”

Download and run models directly: “Browse, download, and load open-weight models from within the app. Harbor handles model management so you can focus on the work, not the setup.”

Cluster for scale: “Connect two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Mac computers and Harbor pools their unified memory into a single inference resource. Run models that exceed any single computer’s capacity, or serve more concurrent requests across your cluster.”

Harbor is currently in a private preview under Apple’s Claris brand, but it seems likely that we’ll see it launch to the public in the weeks and months ahead.

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy: a timeline
snippet: The affair could have ramifications for national security as the U.S. and China race to develop the most advanced AI infrastructure.
fullText:
Nvidia co-founder CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security.

United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China.

The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.

As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.

November 9, 2026: Huang pulls out of various speaking engagements

The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum.

November 9-10, 2026: Details emerge about the business relationships between Nvidia and the alleged spy

Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported. The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips.

Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported. Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang.

In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported.  

November 8, 2026: Trump shows support for Nvidia CEO, calls him a “fine person” 

On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO.

“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said.

When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia, Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.”

November 8, 2026: Huang admits to affair in public message to Nvidia employees; Nvidia board of directors begins investigation 

Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.”

“Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote.

Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day.

November 5, 2026: Three Republican committee chairmen ask Huang for closed-door briefing

Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People’s Republic of China]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.”

October 29, 2026: Jensen Huang publicly revealed to have developed ‘close relationship’ with suspected Chinese spy 

U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year when the New York Times broke the story in late October that the two executives also had a close relationship.

An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.”

Spring 2026: A secret memo circulates in the Trump administration about Nvidia CEO’s alleged relationship with Chinese spy

U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo.

Late 2025: President Trump briefed on U.S. surveillance of Alice Huang and her relationship to Nvidia CEO but does not take action

Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report, U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information.

The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump, has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China.

October 2025: U.S. and Singapore each investigate Megaspeed over possible Chinese export violations

Megaspeed was confirmed to be under investigation by both the U.S. and Singaporean governments in October 2025. As a customer of Nvidia, Megaspeed was suspected of helping Chinese companies get around American embargoes on chip exports.

Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service.

Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. 

These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.”

“NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed — Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules,” the Nvidia spokesperson said at the time.

title: Teens and parents can expect Instagram notifications about AI age estimation
snippet: Meta says it’s expanding its AI age estimation globally to automatically extend Instagram account protections to millions more teenagers. It says parents in the US can also expect to receive notifications later this month … more…
fullText:
Meta says it’s expanding its AI age estimation globally to automatically extend Instagram account protections to millions more teenagers. It says parents in the US can also expect to receive notifications later this month …

Instagram has a number of protections for the accounts of teenagers, but it’s very common for teens to lie about their age in order to circumvent them. Back in May, the company said it would be using AI-powered age estimation to address the problem.

The company said it would use the tool to block users aged below 13, and to ensure that those in the 13 to 17 range had limited accounts. Teen accounts have age-appropriate feeds, limitations on who can interact with them, and default time management tools – though things didn’t get off to the best of starts when a 12-year-old kid fooled it by using an eyebrow pencil to draw a fake moustache.

Meta today says that it is rolling out the (hopefully now eyebrow pencil-proof) tech globally.

We use AI technology to find people we suspect to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday, and place them in Teen Account protections. Since first introducing this technology, we’ve been placing more teens in age-appropriate protections and are encouraged by the results. Based on that success, today we’re expanding this technology globally.

The company goes on to say that parents in the US will receive a notification sometime this month, with a link to a video and an article about the system.

This month, parents in the United States will begin to see an in-feed video on Instagram explaining our approach to ensuring their teens are in age-appropriate protections. The video will link to an article, written by Larry Magid, internet safety advocate and President and CEO of ConnectSafely, detailing our multi-layered age assurance approach, which includes keeping children under 13 off our platforms, providing age appropriate experiences for teens, and informing parents about ways they can partner with us to ensure their teens provide the correct age online.

If you don’t want to wait, you can read the article here.

Meta says the same protections will be rolled out to Threads and Facebook, although I would have thought being on Facebook in the first place is proof that it’s been a while since you were a teenager …

title: Siri co-founder backs Helix for its voice ID tech
snippet: Helix said that its voice ID tech can run on an iPhone 13
fullText:
For years, websites have relied on technology like CAPTCHA to prove that the user on the other end is human. More recently, social media platforms have turned to photos or videos to verify users’ identities. Now, a startup called Helix is betting that voice technology can do the same job, without requiring users to hand over sensitive personal information. 

The voice technology, which can run directly on a user’s device, has attracted backing from Siri co-founder Dag Kittlaus, who will also act as an advisor.

The company raised $6 million in funding in a round led by Chicago Ventures, with participation from BAM Ventures, Aglaé Ventures, Corazon Capital, Tusk Ventures, Yonder Ventures, Rule30, and Brown Alumni Group.

The startup was founded by Alex Oberg, Anna Dorofiyenko, and Mike Hall in 2025. Oberg previously worked at Ticketmaster, which acquired his startup; Dorofiyenko led data science teams at Live Nation and Zillow; and Hall has worked at Nike and Tinder, where he helped develop the initial matching algorithm.

At Ticketmaster, Oberg played a role in creating Verified Fan, which is designed to keep bots out of the platform. As AI advanced, he started thinking along the same lines for a new solution.

“As AI started to come up in the last two years, I was realizing that it’s going to make it increasingly difficult to determine who’s human and who’s not on the Internet. Identity on the Internet’s always been about proxies for identity, right? It’s your email, it’s your phone, it’s your IP address, it’s your device fingerprint, it’s your device ID,” Oberg said.

He noted that with the rise of AI agents like Instinct and Muse, the industry needs to rethink human identity on the internet and rely on biometric signals like voice, which is where Helix comes in.

Its core technology can run directly on a device to determine whether someone is human and estimate their age. The company is also running pilots to explore whether voice can be used a biomarker to detect conditions such as adrunkenness or distress.

The company can deploy its technology to replace or supplement CAPTCHA and help block bot attacks. Helix said that because its model can run locally even on an iPhone 13, the cost of deploying the technology is minimal. The startup said one of its customers is Zeel, an in-home healthcare provider that uses Helix’s tech to verify the identities of providers visiting customers’ homes.

Image Credits:Helix

Oberg said verifying workers, such as cab drivers, is another use case the startup is exploring. He also said that age-verification regulations for social media platforms around the world are forcing users to trade privacy for access. Helix’s voice technology, he said, could offer an alternative.  

“There’s like an avalanche of regulation coming down because essentially society has decided children should not be able to use the Internet as adults. That has created a bit of a strawman argument that everyone needs to trade their privacy for the sake of security and child safety. We are that company that’s saying, nope, don’t agree. It’s a four-second voice challenge,” he said.

The CEO also emphasized the limitations of Helix’s technology, noting that it cannot reliably detect whether someone is lying. He added that its voice technology doesn’t identify individual speakers and claimed that even if the company stores a voiceprint, it cannot be used to reconstruct a person’s voice.

AI-powered fraud is also a growing problem in phone calls. But Helix believes its technology isn’t yet capable of reliably detecting AI agents during live calls.

Siri co-founder Kittlaus said that voice identification technology has finally reached a point where it works reliably, positioning Helix to scale as AI-powered fraud increases. He also said that Helix’s work to compress its models gives the startup a cost advantage.

“What folks at Helix are doing is, instead of teaching computers how to understand speech, these guys are understanding, what the speech of the speaker actually means, what’s going on with them, who they are they lying, are they impaired? That side of it is fascinating to me within the larger picture that I just described,” he told TechCrunch.

title: OpenAI rolls out new business profiles, making ChatGPT just a little bit more like Google
snippet: OpenAI is looking to make ChatGPT a more robust consumer discovery engine, and a host of new features seek to empower businesses to help it do that.
fullText:
In an effort to make ChatGPT an even better consumer discovery engine, OpenAI is launching a host of new features designed to help companies control how users interact with their businesses.

On Tuesday, the company rolled out a Business Hub that will serve as a place where companies can create business profiles that — in a feature that greatly resembles the kind of profiles that Google and other search engines already offer — allow enterprises to verify and update information about their products and services. The feature is currently in beta.

Eligible companies will also be able to create and launch a specialized business agent, which gives ChatGPT users the ability to ask questions about the business and its products.   

“As people turn to AI to discover products, compare options and make decisions, ChatGPT has become the platform for people and businesses to connect through AI,” the company said on Tuesday. “Today’s announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT.”

In a move that calls to mind Google Analytics, the Business Hub will also give users access to limited business insights. These insights will reveal how ChatGPT users interact with their products — including profile views, business mentions, website clicks, and other metrics.

Businesses will have to verify their profiles through a formal process, although the company did not share specifics of what that process would entail. Benji Shomair, OpenAI’s VP of Monetization, told journalists on Monday that there are “multiple verification methods that we use for different types of business in different markets.”

Image Credits:OpenAI

OpenAI previously tried to position ChatGPT as an e-commerce hub by which users could buy products directly. This effort — which used a commission fee system — was viewed as a potentially huge source of revenue and a way to make ChatGPT a more direct Amazon competitor. However, that project ultimately failed to take off and, in March, the company retired the effort, which had even included a “checkout cart” feature.

With the integration of business profiles and intelligence, ChatGPT seems to be attempting to become more like Google, which — since the advent of the internet — has been the place where web users go to understand the companies they want to shop at. It remains to be seen whether this initiative will bear better results than the one that sought to make ChatGPT a direct e-commerce hub.

title: Anthropic launches Claude Meetings to turn workplace discussions into plans and tasks
snippet: As participants talk, Claude can draft the plan being discussed, map out a timeline on a whiteboard, answer questions in the meeting chat, and access connected work apps to retrieve information, such as last year's figures.
fullText:
Anthropic announced new workplace features on Tuesday, including Claude Meetings, which brings Claude into video calls to begin working on tasks while participants are still talking. The company also unveiled Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets.

The launch of Anthropic’s new productivity-focused features comes just a few weeks after OpenAI unveiled a series of workplace tools that allow users to collaborate with ChatGPT to do things like visualize company information and create presentations, as both companies compete to turn their products into office suites of sorts to take on Microsoft and Google. Meta is also joining the competition with its Muse AI agent, which can build mini-apps on the fly to help users complete specific tasks.

With Claude Meetings, teams can add Claude to a video call as a visible participant. Claude then follows the conversation and gets to work on tasks in real time. As participants talk, it can draft the plan being discussed, map out a timeline on a whiteboard, answer questions in the meeting chat, and access connected work apps to retrieve information, such as last year’s figures. After the call, the meeting notes, action items, and other materials Claude created are available in claude.ai.

The work that comes out of a meeting usually starts after everyone hangs up, but with this new feature, teams can turn discussions into actions in real time, Anthropic says.

Claude identifies itself as a meeting participant and posts a notice in the meeting chat. It won’t join calls with external guests unless authorized by an admin, and will automatically leave if an external guest joins. 

Claude Meetings is launching in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. At launch, it works with Google Meet, with support for additional plans expected to follow.

Image Credits:Anthropic

As for Claude Whiteboards, Anthropic describes the feature as a collaborative board where teams can talk through a plan and have Claude turn it into an organized visual workspace with timelines and deadlines.

The company notes that many people already brainstorm with Claude, but that in order to share their results with others, they would have to copy-paste them somewhere else. Now, a team can work directly with Claude on the same board in real time.

When the brainstorm is done, Claude can turn the board into a doc or a slide deck. Additionally, Whiteboards also work inside Claude Meetings, so the board builds while people talk, Anthropic says. 

Claude Whiteboards is available in beta on paid plans, on web, desktop, and mobile.

The company also launched Claude Sheets, which lets teams create and collaboratively edit spreadsheets with Claude. A team can ask it to build a campaign tracker or hiring budget, and Claude will then generate a working spreadsheet.

Image Credits:Anthropic

Anthropic says Claude handles the initial setup of trackers and budgets, while allowing teams to continue refining and updating the same spreadsheet. Each spreadsheet can include multiple tabs, formulas, formatting, and dropdown menus. Claude also makes edits directly in cells alongside the team, and outlines each change so users can see what it did.

Claude Sheets is available in beta on paid plans, on web, desktop and mobile.

Anthropic also announced that Claude Data, formerly known as Claude Dashboards, is now generally available. The feature connects Claude to systems that companies use to keep their numbers, like a data warehouse or CRM. Users can ask questions, and Claude responds with dashboards, written data stories, or narrated videos.

Additionally, the company announced interactive connectors that open the full version of apps like Adobe, Atlassian, and HubSpot inside Claude. Anthropic notes that teams can now open these apps directly alongside their Claude conversations and ask the assistant to work within them, essentially bringing existing workflows into the same workspace.

title: Google and Adobe partner to add app integration in Google Drive, Gemini
snippet: Google Drive will soon prompt users to switch to Adobe Acrobat while viewing PDFs, and Gemini will get a few new tricks powered by the company’s creative suite. more…
fullText:
Google Drive will soon prompt users to switch to Adobe Acrobat while viewing PDFs, and Gemini will get a few new tricks powered by the company’s creative suite.

The pipeline from PDFs opened in Google Drive and Gmail to Adobe Acrobat is notoriously strained. That goes for any PDF viewer, but as soon as certain tools are necessary, a large number of users rely on Adobe’s products to edit and store documents.

Google announced plans to ease the process. According to a press release today, Google will be adding a “direct pathway” from Google Drive and Gmail in Adobe Acrobat. Acrobat will be suggested to users within the services, which will likely act as a quick transfer sort of feature. It doesn’t seem to indicate users will see any Adobe PDF editing tools within Google Drive. Google Drive has notoriously fallen short in this regard.

The partnership announcement also means Gemini will get access to some of Adobe’s creative tools. Further detail isn’t clear, but that includes Gemini, Gemini Enterprise, and Google AI Mode in Search. It sounds like the integration will allow users to edit or manage PDFs and other files straight from Google’s AI interfaces.

	

It’s not just PDFs and Google Drive; Adobe’s Photoshop gets a shout, too. Expected sometimes in the future, we may see  more powerful image editing powered by Gemini within Adobe Photoshop, as opposed to the current models and limitations within. Gemini Nano Banana models are currently in use, but AI generation and editing could go further with a more focused effort. Google says the push “could enable near-real-time edits,” but there’s no concrete timeline set for when we could see that.

That goes for each of these byproducts of the new partnership. Google Drive and Gmail integration with Adobe Acrobat will likely be the first to roll out, with Gemini features to follow shortly after.

title: iOS 27.3 adds new setting to bypass website cookie popups (eventually)
snippet: iOS 27.3 is currently in beta and packed with new features, including a ‘Global Privacy Control’ setting in Safari that could someday put an end to cookie consent pop-ups. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.3 is currently in beta and packed with new features, including a ‘Global Privacy Control’ setting in Safari that could someday put an end to cookie consent pop-ups.

Safari has new ‘Global Privacy Control’ setting in iOS 27.3 for automatic cookie opt-outs

Apple has several big changes coming to Safari in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3. The browser is adding Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and new Siri AI powers.

But iOS 27.3 has another Safari feature that’s hidden away in Settings: a new ‘Global Privacy Control’ option.

Inside Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Safari ⇾ Advanced you’ll find the ‘Use Global Privacy Control’ setting. Apple describes it this way:

Safari can ask websites to not sell or share your data. This may cause some websites to not function properly or work at all.

The beta also links to a support document where users can find more information, but it’s currently a broken link. The document will likely be published on iOS 27.3’s release day.

As noted by Nick Heer on his site Pixel Envy, this Global Privacy Control setting is “effectively a replacement for Do Not Track with legal muscle that should permit you to indicate your tracking preference one time and then, theoretically, never again see a cookie consent banner.”

Ultimately though, the dream of automatically declining cookie consents has a long road to reality. Websites have to add support for Global Privacy Control (which some have already done, but most haven’t). And GPC currently only has legal muscle in five US states.

That said, the addition of a Global Privacy Control setting in iOS 27.3 is a good start. And hopefully it means that in a few years, many Safari users don’t need to see cookie consent popups anymore.

fullText:
Some of the most impressive tech that Adobe showcases at its annual Max conference each year is the experimental features it’s developing, and the latest of those tools are being announced today: they can transform images into explorable 3D scenes, design AI characters by talking to them, and turn photo editing into a copy/paste process.

The first (and weirdest, in my opinion) is Project Screen Test, which is designed to make AI-generated characters easier to develop and use for video content. Instead of just describing how the character should sound and behave in text prompts, the tool lets you talk to the character and direct them in an audition-like environment. You start by describing some base personality traits, such as “anxious, shy, awkward,” and giving the character a voice, either by selecting a preset, describing how it sounds in a prompt, or uploading sample audio for it to reference.

You can then expand its persona in further detail by conversing with the character as if you’re talking on FaceTime, outlining its backstory, temperament, goals, flaws, fears, movement quirks and more. Once you’re happy, the tool lets you generate animated screen tests with the character by describing an environment or scenario you want to put them in.

This is currently a standalone creative exercise, and it’s not clear how (or if) it could feature in any of Adobe’s existing AI video tools. The results provided a more identifiable and consistent personality compared to many soulless animated AI characters I’ve seen, but that’s the entire reason this exists — AI video generation provides far less creative control compared to traditional animation, where every aspect of a character is included with absolute intention.

There’s also Project Sight Span, which reframes photographs and images by turning them into a 3D environment that you can navigate through and reposition. The 3D space generates objects and backgrounds that are outside of the original frame, but feel like a natural part of the image, even if you’re turning to see what’s behind you. While the visuals in the 3D environment are pixelated and ill–defined, the resolution quality is restored when you select your chosen angle.

Sight Span works with any flat image, including photos, paintings, and illustrations, and can preserve and replicate artistic styles. Even repositioned tattoos and facial features in photographs remain surprisingly recognizable and true to the original reference. It’s a bit like a version of Apple’s Spatial Reframing feature on steroids: you can reposition more aggressively and change the shooting point entirely if you want, but it also feels far less deserving of being called a photo afterward.

Project Sound Bender is an AI audio mixing feature that lets you customize sound effects as if you’re clicking your cursor around a color wheel. It works by uploading a video clip and then describing your desired audio in a text prompt, such as “bubbling sci-fi cauldron noises.” Sound Bender then generates sound effects and automatically syncs it to the video, and provides a square sound canvas that lets you adjust the noises in real time. Each corner of the canvas will automatically assign a relevant AI-generated sound, such as dense gurgling with popping bubbles, rumbling boiling rocks, pitched bloops, and crackling electric fire. You can drag your cursor around the canvas to select which noises stand out the most, or customize each corner with different sound effects.

Adobe also showcased Project Rinse Repeat, which lets you copy edits and then automatically apply them to other objects or people in the same photo. For example, if you painstakingly airbrush out acne or blemishes on one person, Rinse Repeat will adapt your specific changes to anyone else in a group of people who need similar touchups. It can also be used to add shadows to products in marketing graphics, even if the objects are different shapes and sizes. Rinse Repeat is built around Photoshop, and the edits you apply to other subjects remain fully editable because the tool recreates them with native Photoshop tools.

These “sneaks” are tech previews of capabilities that might eventually be developed into tools for Adobe’s Creative Cloud apps or Firefly platform, so there’s no guarantee that they’ll graduate into being available features. Almost all of these projects are built around Adobe’s generative AI developments, however, and given AI tools now play a central role in the company’s growth strategy, it’s likely that at least some of the experiments will see an official launch. As wacky or fun as these AI experiments are, they’re also an omen. If they’re useful enough, that means AI may eventually replace the tools and stock libraries that creative professionals currently use, regardless of how complex their feelings are about the technology.

A notable theme across these sneaks is making complicated photo editing, filmmaking, and audio mixing workflows feel more accessible and intuitive, adapting them into something that’s more interactive and easy to use. In some cases the features almost seem like toys, but with the benefit of allowing you to make practical changes to creative projects.

“Making these interactions more intuitive is also about giving experienced creatives more precise control,” senior principle Adobe research scientist Gautham Mysore, told The Verge. “Sound Bender’s sonic exploration capability and Sight Span’s camera positioning are examples of how professionals could apply their judgment and refine a result more directly. That connection between creative intent and control is a big part of what we’re exploring.”

Some of the most impressive tech that Adobe showcases at its annual Max conference each year is the experimental features it’s developing, and the latest of those tools are being announced today: they can transform images into explorable 3D scenes, design AI characters by talking to them, and turn photo editing into a copy/paste process.

The first (and weirdest, in my opinion) is Project Screen Test, which is designed to make AI-generated characters easier to develop and use for video content. Instead of just describing how the character should sound and behave in text prompts, the tool lets you talk to the character and direct them in an audition-like environment. You start by describing some base personality traits, such as “anxious, shy, awkward,” and giving the character a voice, either by selecting a preset, describing how it sounds in a prompt, or uploading sample audio for it to reference.

title: From Green Screen to Gray Box: AI Is Stepping Onto the Hollywood Sound Stage
snippet: A movie set with blank, neutral walls can be filled in with AI-generated backgrounds and lighting.
fullText:
On screen, a woman runs toward a cliff and peers anxiously over the edge, teetering as she looks down at a perilous mountain dotted with boulders, her hair flying in the wind.

She’s not, though. I can see her from where I’m standing in the middle of a Disney sound stage in Los Angeles. She’s standing in a “gray box,” a small, walled-off space on the studio floor, neutral-colored walls speckled with small cross marks for positioning. She’s next to a stack of blue-carpeted boxes that serve as a stand-in for whatever large prop that post-production decides to add in digitally later. 

A camera is pointing at her, following her every move. And an almost instant rendering on a screen has placed her on that cliff, perfectly lit, wind tousling her hair, thanks in part to AI.

			

More from CNET

Green screens and blue screens have been used for more than half a century in TV and filmmaking, allowing post-production crews to insert visual effects and backgrounds behind the actors. But the bright hue can reflect onto objects and skin, and constant adjustments to the backdrop are needed when the director wants to switch to a new angle of the shot.

Filming in a gray box like the one I’m standing next to offers more flexible shots. And combining that with AI-generated or assisted backgrounds speeds up post-production, according to entertainment studio Promise Advanced Imagination, which showcased its filming product during the Disney Accelerator Demo Day last week.

Even the lighting changes instantly to match the sets being generated or assisted by AI.Disney/Screenshots by CNET

Setting up shots takes less time in gray boxes than it does with a green screen background, Promise co-founder and chief creative officer Dave Clark told me, giving crews more time to be creative because “they’re not bogged down by having to take 2 to 3 hours to change the setup.”

“You’re able to still capture the right performance and the right blocking … this allows me to just focus on the story, focus on the creative and not worry,” Clark said. “You can get multiple takes because you can get them faster, you don’t have to worry about moving the crew, you don’t have to worry about changing lights, everything stays consistent so I can just focus on the story.”

Crews can save time while filming by using these gray boxes. More time (and cost) is saved during post-production by using AI tools to help fill in the backgrounds and replace lighting and objects. 

While some environments are wholly AI-created, most are made by human 3D renderers and visual effects artists working with AI as one of their tools. Using AI to help fill in backgrounds lowers the cost of production but still ensures it has the size and scale of high-quality productions, Clark says, with production companies needing a lot less capital to produce pilots. 

Clark, who’s also a director, insists that everything still “goes through the hands of human artists,” however.

“Much like Disney or Pixar, the process begins with the script, then it goes into storyboard and then (filming),” Clark said. “I think that traditional mindset and that traditional skill set that you only learn over decades of experience is really what amplifies this technology and lets it work for your creative capabilities.”

As filmmaking and animation studios increasingly explore the use of AI tools in streamlining productions, there have been concerns that human jobs will be removed, including across actors, animators, writers, set designers and more.

David Min, vice president of Disney Innovation, told me this system just fills in the background of movies, which is already done with other technologies, such as green screens. This just makes it easier and faster, since lighting changes can even be done in post-production. It means the people on set can focus just on the performances and direction. There will always be directors, writers and actors, he said.

Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro agrees, saying “technology itself is not the goal.”

“We’re being very aggressive about exploring emerging technologies,” D’Amaro said at the event. “It’s to put it in the hands of our creators … to create these incredible and immersive stories.”

Corinne Reichert/CNET

During the demo day at Walt Disney Studios in Burbank, California, Promise CEO George Strompoulis explained to the media that the company — which bills itself as a generative AI studio developing movies, series and visual effects to “support human artistry” — is made up of four major components: Promise Studios can help produce “studio-quality features at a fraction of the cost and timeline”; then there’s the Muse AI technology platform workflow software; the Curious Refuge AI Filmmaking academy, to serve as “a pipeline of the best artists in the world” and to “upscale” existing film industry workers; and The Generation Company, which is Promise’s AI visual effects business.

Promise has done some testing with the Disney teams, and has a series pilot in production with another studio.

“I think it’s easy for people to have the misconception that there’s an AI button that could just make a movie,” said Rob Bredow, senior vice president of creative innovation at Disney. “That is not the approach that Disney’s taking; it’s not the approach that Promise is taking, which is why this has been a good collaboration.”

I watch the screens as the same woman from the cliff edge now appears to be crouching fearfully next to a blown-out car as explosions rain debris around her. 

She’s still right in front of me, squatting next to those blue boxes in the Disney studio sound stage, camera trained on her. I also watch her pick up a screwdriver from the floor. On screen, it transforms into a mysterious scroll out of a Lara Croft-esque adventure movie.

“The ability to do this at cinematic-quality level is something that we’re at the beginning stages of now,” Clark said. “You not only need great filmmakers; you need creative technologists, you need artists who are masters in the AI tools.”

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Corinne Reichert
						

						

							Senior Editor						
					

											

								

											Corinne Reichert (she/her) grew up in Sydney, Australia and moved to California in 2019. She holds degrees in law and communications, and currently writes news, analysis and features for CNET across the topics of electric vehicles, broadband networks, mobile devices, big tech, artificial intelligence, home technology and entertainment. In her spare time, she watches soccer games and F1 races, and goes to Disneyland as often as possible.
