title: Today’s macOS updates fix security gap involving eMudhra certificates
snippet: Apple today released macOS updates that address a security gap involving compromised eMudhra certificates, after initially blocking them in Safari, Mail, and other apps in October. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple today released macOS updates that address a security gap involving compromised eMudhra certificates, after initially blocking them in Safari, Mail, and other apps in October. Here are the details.

A bit of context

A few weeks ago, Mozilla reported that private keys of eight intermediate certificate authorities operated by eMudhra, an Indian digital certification company, had been compromised.

In essence, these certificates are used to establish trust in digital certificates that verify website identities and enable secure connections.

With access to the compromised private keys, bad actors could potentially create fraudulent certificates that appear legitimate, allowing them to impersonate websites and intercept sensitive user information.

In response to the compromise, Apple began automatically blocking the affected certificates on October 19, followed by additional protections on October 23.

These changes were delivered through automatic certificate configuration updates, meaning users didn’t need to install a macOS update to be protected.

While these measures protected Safari, Mail, and apps that use Apple’s networking and security frameworks, they didn’t cover all of macOS, as certain command-line tools, including curl and git, could still accept the compromised certificates.

At the time, Apple published a support article with instructions for administrators to manually address this remaining security gap, while promising a fix in a future macOS update.

Today, Apple updated the document to confirm that the fix is now available.

Apple closes remaining eMudhra security gap

As Apple explains, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, and macOS 15.8.3, released earlier today, prevent the affected command-line tools from accepting the compromised certificates, eliminating the need for administrators to manually address the issue.

The updates also remove five root CA certificates from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, including three additional eMudhra certificates that weren’t part of Apple’s original manual workaround.

Still, for users who are unable to install the latest macOS updates, Apple continues to provide instructions for manually addressing the issue in its support document, along with the names and SHA-256 fingerprints of the 12 affected certificates and five root CA certificates removed by the updates.

Apple also notes that “some apps and tools include their own list of root CA certificates and don’t use Apple’s block or /etc/ssl/cert.pem,” and advises users to contact the developer of those apps and tools.

title: watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love
snippet: watchOS 27.3 arrived this week in beta alongside iOS 27.3, with a major new feature for the latest Apple Watch models: Siri Recap, which I’m already really loving. more…
fullText:
watchOS 27.3 arrived this week in beta alongside iOS 27.3, with a major new feature for the latest Apple Watch models: Siri Recap, which I’m already really loving.

Siri Recap in watchOS 27.3 and iOS 27.3 makes the Apple Watch a powerful AI tool

If you bought an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 this fall, there are two exclusive new features coming in watchOS 27.3: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Both ‘Audio Intelligence’ features were announced at Apple’s September keynote, but just debuted in beta this week.

Siri Recap in particular has stirred some controversy. Here’s what the feature does, per Apple:

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Siri Recaps can be set to automatically delete after a period of up to 7 days unless you choose to explicitly save them.

It’s understandable why users would be concerned. Once enabled, Siri Recap can turn your Apple Watch into a device that’s always listening and often takes notes on what it hears.

This article isn’t about making the privacy case for the feature. You can read Apple’s privacy protections here. Briefly though, key details include: there’s no speaker attribution or logging of sensitive information like financial data, authentication data, or personal identifiers; no audio is stored or recorded; the feature is opt-in; and you can set times or places where it stays disabled.

Speaking strictly of the functionality of Siri Recap itself, however, I’ve been very impressed.

My experience with Siri Recap so far

I enabled Siri Recap after installing the iOS and watchOS 27.3 betas on Tuesday. When I checked the first recaps on Wednesday inside the Siri app, I was blown away.

Siri had created a record of the things I’d done Tuesday afternoon and evening with remarkable accuracy and detail, as seen above.

One example that especially shocked me: after shopping for Christmas decorations with my family, Siri documented the size of a table runner we looked at. The thing is, I had no memory of anyone even mentioning its size. My wife must have, but despite me missing it, Siri wrote it down.

Another fun one: Thursday morning during breakfast, my son wanted to listen some music on our HomePod. Later that day, I found that the songs we’d listened to were saved at the bottom of my latest recap.

It’s still very early days with Siri Recap, which is only in beta right now, but what I’ve seen this week has been really exciting. And so far at least, I’ve seen zero information in a recap that I’d consider too sensitive to be included.

What’s your take on Siri Recap? Have you given it a try? Let us know in the comments.

title: iOS 27.2 adds three new ways to customize your iPhone
snippet: iOS 27.2 launched last week with a lot of new features, and also several ways you can customize your iPhone. Here’s what’s new for iPhone personalization. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 launched last week with a lot of new features, and also several ways you can customize your iPhone. Here’s what’s new for iPhone personalization.

#1: Exclude apps from Siri and Search

Inside Settings ⇾ Siri there’s a new ‘Excluded Apps’ section in iOS 27.2. This makes it easier than ever to remove certain apps from being accessible to Siri, Search, and more. Apple says:

Apps added to the list below will be excluded from Siri, Search, and suggestions.

With Siri AI, Siri can do more than ever before. But if there are certain apps you want off-limits, whether for privacy reasons or otherwise, you can add them to this list. For example, if there’s an app with a similar name to something else, adding it to the ‘Excluded Apps’ list can ensure Siri won’t mistakenly think you’re referencing that app anymore.

#2: Customize Messages suggestions

iOS 27.2 adds a new Messages feature called Suggestions that I’m a big fan of. When relevant content is detected in a conversation, you might see a Suggestion appear underneath a message. For example, if a friend asks you to do them a favor, you might see “Add to Reminders” below the message.

By default there are five supported categories of Suggestions:

Add to Calendar

Add to Reminders

Add to Notes

Show in Maps

Flights and Packages

You can fully customize these to your own preferences and needs. Just go to Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Messages ⇾ Suggested Actions to disable whichever Suggestions you don’t want to see.

#3: Apple TV user profiles

Historically, Apple TV has only ever supported user profiles on tvOS. It’s an odd limitation considering every other streaming service offers profiles across platforms.

But finally with iOS 27.2, profiles are now available on iPhone too, letting you customize the content in the Apple TV app based on who’s watching.

Choosing a profile not only gives you personalized recommendations from Apple TV, it also lets you keep the ‘Continue Watching’ queue separate for each person. And if you’re setting up a profile for a child, you can set content restrictions too.

title: I asked every TV manufacturer 17 questions about how they spy on you

fullText:
Every TV company is spying on you, not just LG. Like other tech companies, they collect lots of information, and while some is necessary for products to work, not all of it is — and could include details you’d prefer to keep private. Many customers are concerned about how TVs and streaming devices might be spying: listening to what you say, taking screenshots of everything you watch, storing sensitive information on your TV, and sharing your data with the cloud.

To find out what TV and streaming device companies are doing, I decided to ask every one to explain itself. I put together 17 yes-or-no questions, like “Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?” so that companies couldn’t just link to a confusing and legalese-ridden privacy policy. TV users deserve to know the answers.

Company representatives providing responses

Amazon: Eric Sveum, PR manager

Apple: Emily Ewing, public relations manager

Google: Alex García-Kummert, spokesperson

LG Electronics: Chris De Maria, director of public relations

Roku: Sarah Novatt, spokesperson

Samsung: Frank Giancamilli, corporate communications senior manager

TCL: Rob Manfredo, head of communications and events

One month ago, I invited 11 companies, including Amazon, Apple, Google, Hisense, LG, Panasonic, Roku, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Walmart’s Vizio to share those answers. We now have answers from the top three TV manufacturers as well as every major streaming device company. Some companies declined to answer. Below, you can see and compare how each company answered (or failed to answer) each question and then decide how you feel. (One company, Hisense, ignored our emails entirely.)

As you’ll see them say, some of this data collection is opt-in, and you can often opt out. We know that many TVs use automatic content recognition (ACR) to figure out potentially everything we’re watching, and use that information to tailor ads, gather audience metrics, and serve up content recommendations based on our viewing habits. But though it sometimes seems like it’s required during the cavalcade of agreements thrown at us during setup, you can generally stop ACR even after you’ve agreed to it.

Opting out might not be as effective as it should be, however. A recent Northeastern University study found that Walmart’s Vizio kept on sending data after an opt-out (Vizio told me it was “routine operational data used to support the Vizio experience,” not ACR), while traffic with both Samsung and Roku was limited, but not stopped completely.

Below are the answers to our 17 questions. You will notice that some companies would not answer yes or no. We’ve also noted where companies declined to answer at all or ignored the questions. If any company becomes willing to directly answer our questions, we’ll add their responses.

1. Do your TVs ever use their embedded microphones, or the microphones in their remotes, to listen to sound in a customer’s home?

Amazon:

No. Fire TV includes voice functionality to help customers use their devices and get to content they love and fast, not to surveil homes. The microphones on our voice remotes are designed to only work when the mic button on the remote is physically pressed. And TVs with hands-free Alexa are designed to detect the wake word (and only the wake word) before connecting to Alexa. No audio is stored or sent to the cloud unless the device detects the wake word. Customers can also turn off the microphones at any time. Every Fire TV smart television that has microphones also has a physical button or switch that disables the microphone.

Apple:

Apple TV 4K will use its far-field microphones and the Always On Processor strictly to listen for the Siri wake word. The Always On Processor does not process or act on any other sounds in the home. Users have full control over this and can turn off “Siri” or “Hey Siri” as a wake word, or disable Siri entirely. When using the Siri Remote, users must actively press and hold the microphone button for it to start listening.

Google:

If Google Assistant or Gemini is enabled or available, microphones (built-in hands-free ‘Hey Google’ or remote push-to-talk button) listen for activation triggers. Microphones remain in passive standby until triggered by hotword or button press.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

Voice recognition is off by default and operates only if the user has opted in by accepting the Voice Information Agreement. Even if the user has opted in, they need to take additional steps for the microphone to be used. They must either press the microphone button on the remote control or they can use Hands-free Voice Control on supported models.

Hands-free Voice Control is disabled unless a user opts into this feature and then uses a wake-word. Wake-word detection is performed locally on the TV. If no wake word is detected, the audio is processed locally, promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

While Roku TVs don’t have built-in microphones, some Roku remotes do. Standard voice remotes listen only while the mic button is held, and hands-free remotes can be switched off.

Samsung:

No, for private monitoring. Samsung TVs do not listen to or record private conversations.

The TV’s embedded microphone only listens locally for the specific wake-up word (like “Hi, Bixby”) and ignores all other sounds, while the remote control microphone only activates when the customer physically presses the button.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

Some TCL TVs and remotes have microphones. Users can activate those microphones to use voice assistance features provided through third-party operating systems or applications. Those third parties control whether the voice features are available and how they are used, under their own terms and privacy policies.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

2. Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?

Amazon:

No.

Apple:

Apple did not provide a direct answer to this question.

Google:

[Recorded audio and/or transcripts based on audio are] stored only if ‘Voice & Audio Activity’ (VAA) is explicitly enabled under Google Account Web & App Activity. Voice & Audio Activity is off by default. If VAA is off, voice requests are processed in real-time and not saved to the Google Account.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

If voice recognition is enabled (by opting in) and activated (by pushing the remote control’s microphone button or using the wake word), certain information generated as part of a specific voice recognition interaction may be stored locally on the TV to support voice-related features. Depending on the interaction, this may include Speech-to-text results derived from a user’s voice command.

Audio used for wake-word detection is processed locally on the TV and, if no wake word is detected, captured audio is promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Voice commands made via voice-enabled remotes may be retained to improve voice features and provide support, consistent with Roku’s privacy policy. Users can opt out in their Roku account privacy settings.

Samsung:

No. Samsung Smart TVs do not store voice recordings or transcripts on the device.

However, on secure servers, voice commands and transcripts are stored only to process requests and improve voice assistant services.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

TCL does not collect audio data from TCL TV or remote microphones, or from the use of third-party voice features.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

3. Do your TVs transmit any audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?

Amazon:

When customers speak to Alexa by pressing the mic button on the remote or using their chosen wake word, a recording of the request is sent to Amazon’s cloud, where a text transcript of the request is created to help Alexa provide a response. No audio is captured without the customer invoking Alexa—either by pressing the mic button or saying the wake word—and customers can easily review exactly what they asked and what Alexa heard, delete their recording, or even choose not to save them at all.

Apple:

Siri AI processes user requests using on-device processing, and when a request needs more powerful AI models, it extends those same on-device privacy protections to the cloud through a groundbreaking infrastructure called Private Cloud Compute (PCC). When Private Cloud Compute is handling users’ requests, their personal data is not stored nor made accessible to Apple, or anyone else, and outside experts can verify this privacy promise at any time.

For moments when users ask a question that requires up‑to‑date information, Siri AI can go out to the web and find it, then use Private Cloud Compute to generate an answer. Searches and requests are associated with a random identifier — a long string of letters and numbers — not a user’s Apple Account.

Google:

If Voice & Audio Activity is turned on, when voice features are activated (via hotword or remote button), captured audio or transcripts are transmitted to Google cloud servers for processing and fulfilling commands. If VAA is turned off, these are deleted.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

Yes, but only if voice recognition has been enabled (by opting in) and activated (by pushing the remote control microphone button or using the wake word). When voice recognition is activated, the TV displays an on-screen indication that voice recognition is active and listening for the user’s command. Once the user finishes the voice command, the command is transmitted to our server, where it is converted into text and processed to respond to the command.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku: 

Roku TVs don’t have microphones. Voice-enabled remotes let people control their Roku devices by voice, as described in our privacy policy.

Samsung:

No, for ambient or background listening. Samsung TVs do not passively monitor, record, or transmit audio from your home. Audio is only captured and transmitted when you actively initiate a voice command (such as pressing the microphone button on your remote or using the wake word). This voice input is processed securely to fulfill your requests, improve services, and support connected features under our voice privacy policies.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

TCL did not provide a direct answer to this question.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

4. Do your TVs collect any screenshots, screen recordings, or video recordings of what viewers are watching?

Amazon:

No.

Apple:

Apple TV 4K does not use automatic content recognition (ACR), nor does it collect screenshots, screen recordings, or video recordings of what viewers are watching. If a user chooses to ask a question about what’s on their screen, that data is processed by Siri AI. This feature is only initiated by a direct user request.

Google:

Google TV platform software does not utilize Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) to capture on-screen video or screenshots. (Note: Third-party TV hardware OEMs may install separate ACR software, but Google TV OS itself does not).

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

No. ACR in LG TVs does not collect or store screenshots, screen images, screen recordings, or video recordings from the TV. Instead, it uses audio fingerprints generated from content audio using the TV’s internal soundboard (not a speaker) to identify the content being viewed.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

No.

Samsung:

No. Samsung TVs do not capture or store screenshots, screen recordings, or video recordings of what viewers watch.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

TCL did not provide a direct answer to this question.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

5. Do your TVs store or transmit data on what content viewers watch or listen to through the TV?

Amazon:

Yes. For example, customers can opt in to allow Fire TV to collect certain viewing information like what shows they’ve watched in third-party apps to improve and personalize their experience, including by displaying shows and movies in a Continue Watching row on the Fire TV home screen. Customers can manage that setting anytime via their device’s Privacy Settings.

Apple:

Apple did not provide a direct answer to this question.

Google:

[Google TV] stores and transmits viewing history, watchlists, and app interactions for rentals/purchases on GTV and FreePlay. We do not have viewing history on third party apps.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

If the user has agreed to the Viewing Information Agreement, viewing information may be collected or processed in certain circumstances, including the following:

- ACR: Where ACR is available and enabled, ACR-related information may be collected and processed to identify content being viewed from supported sources. ACR uses audio fingerprinting technology to identify content rather than collecting screenshots, screen recordings, video recordings, voice recordings, or other audio recordings from the TV. To operate ACR services, LG may process content-identification fingerprints together with device information, content source information, network information, and consent settings needed to support the feature. ACR is optional and is turned off by default, and users can disable the feature at any time through the TV settings. ACR does not operate within third-party streaming apps.

- LG Channels: When a user streams content through LG Channels, information about the content being viewed is processed and sent to our servers so we can provide the requested streaming service.

- Voice Recognition: When users make voice commands, those commands and current viewing information (such as channel number and program name, and whether the source is an antenna or set-top-box) are sent to the server to process the voice commands and provide appropriate responses.

- Usage Information: Certain viewing information may also be collected as part of usage information relating to how the user interacts with the TV and its services, such as information about content selected for viewing or channels the user switches to.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

We collect streaming activity as described in our privacy policy. Smart TV Experience, which can identify other content on screen, is off by default in the US and is enabled only if the user opts in.

Samsung:

Yes, but only for TV programming and app viewing history. Samsung TVs do not monitor or transmit your personal files or private media.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

TCL collects limited data only for diagnostics and product improvement from some models of TCL Smart TVs. This collection is disclosed to users at setup and in TCL’s privacy notice, uses pseudonymization to prevent user profiling, and can be turned off by the user.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

6. Do your TVs collect any telemetry about where users are clicking, selecting, tapping, or otherwise looking when using the TV?

Amazon:

Fire TV collects data about how customers use the device, such as navigating the home screen or opening apps, to provide and improve features. Customers can opt out of certain data collection and use via Privacy Settings.

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

[Google TV] collects device navigation telemetry (button presses, navigation clicks, app launch/exit events) under ‘Usage & Diagnostics’ settings to assess system health and reliability. Does not store “hovering” or “highlight” states.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

To provide and improve smart services, the LG smart TV may collect certain basic usage information about how users interact with the TV, such as the features, menu items, apps, or services they select or use. LG does not collect information about a user’s activity within third-party apps. LG does not track where users are looking when using the TV.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

We collect standard usage data, such as button presses and menu selections, to run and improve the product.

Samsung:

For menu interactions and viewing selections, interactions (like clicks or selections) are analyzed primarily in aggregate to improve the user experience and service recommendations.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

TCL does not collect data at the device level regarding what viewers watch, except when a user requests remote diagnostic support, in which case the information is used to fix the problem the user reported.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

7. Do your TVs transmit any information that could identify the location of their owner, including their public IP address, Wi-Fi network SSID, GPS coordinates, and/or actual street address?

Amazon:

Yes. For example, IP addresses are transmitted as part of normal network communication, for your device to communicate with the internet and deliver content. There is no GPS hardware on Fire TV devices.

Apple:

Apple did not provide a direct answer to this question.

Google:

[Google TV] transmits public IP address, Wi-Fi scan data (SSID/BSSID), and account/device regional configuration to determine approximate or precise device location.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

To provide Smart TV functionality, the TV must be connected to the internet. If the TV is connected to the internet, then like any other internet-connected device, the Smart TV will transmit its IP address. The IP address may be used to determine its approximate geographic location to provide services appropriate for the user’s region.

Separately, when ACR is enabled, the TV’s IP address and information about nearby Wi-Fi networks, such as MAC addresses and signal strength, may be used to estimate the TV’s approximate location as part of the ACR service. This ACR-related location processing is limited to ACR and is not used generally across other TV services.

The TV does not contain a GPS module and does not use GPS to determine its location.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Roku TVs don’t collect GPS data. Like any connected device, they transmit a public IP address, which may be used for approximate location, among other purposes, per our privacy policy.

Samsung:

No, for physical locations. Samsung TVs do not collect or transmit GPS coordinates, Wi-Fi SSIDs, or your physical street address. However, for network connection, the TV must transmit its public IP address to connect to the internet and run basic features (like the Smart Hub and software updates). This IP address is only used for network communication and general region detection (like country or state), not to pinpoint your actual address.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

To provide location-based services, TCL collects IP address and Wi-Fi network name (SSID) information, as described in the terms and privacy policy to which users agree when they initially set up their TV. TCL uses this information only to identify a country or city in order to deliver services, not the user’s specific location. TCL TVs have no GPS modules, and TCL does not collect street addresses through the TV. If a user creates a TCL account on a TCL Google TV, TCL collects an email address and age to confirm that the user is an adult. Apart from that, TCL’s practice is not to collect personally identifiable information from its televisions.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

8. Do your TVs store or transmit any other potentially personally identifying information about their owners, including their name, age, gender, orientation, and demographic?

Amazon:

Fire TV devices are associated with customers’ Amazon account, which includes their name and account information.

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

Because Google TV requires a Google Account for smart functionality, linked profile information (name, email, age, gender) is accessed, stored, and transmitted for personalization and age-restriction policies.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

When creating an LG account, the user provides their name, email address and date of birth (to confirm applicable age requirements). If a user creates an LG account from their Smart TV, the TV will temporarily store and then transmit this information to LG’s servers.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Users provide account information, such as name and email, when they create a Roku account, as described in our privacy policy.

Samsung:

Samsung SmartTVs do not collect/store or transmit name, age, gender, orientation or demographic information.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

If a user creates a TCL account on a TCL Google TV, TCL collects an email address and age to confirm that the user is an adult. Apart from that, TCL’s practice is not to collect personally identifiable information from its televisions.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

9. Does your company store any of the kinds of information in Question 7 or 8 in the cloud or other remote servers? If so, which?

Amazon:

Yes. Information transmitted to Amazon’s cloud is encrypted in transit and stored securely.

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

Both location data (IP address/Wi-Fi) and Google Account profile data (name, email address, age/gender demographics) are stored on Google’s cloud servers linked to your account profile.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

Yes. Information such as IP addresses, device-level identifiers, and, if a user has an LG Account, account information such as name, email address, and date of birth, is stored on LG’s cloud or other remote servers. When ACR is enabled, the ACR-related information described above, including nearby Wi-Fi network information such as MAC addresses and signal strength, may also be stored on remote servers.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Data may be stored on Roku’s servers or with major cloud providers to operate the service, as described in our privacy policy.

Samsung:

Yes. The information described above is stored in encrypted or hashed form within secure cloud infrastructure managed by Samsung.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

The limited information described above is stored with cloud service providers, including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud, subject to TCL’s terms and privacy policy.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

10. Do your TVs transmit any information about the other devices on an owner’s home Wi-Fi network?

Amazon:

No.

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

[Google TV] discovers nearby Cast-enabled devices and smart home hardware via local network protocols (mDNS, SSDP, Matter/Thread) and transmits device discovery/connectivity logs.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

To support connectivity capabilities, LG smart TVs identify other devices on the user’s Wi-Fi network. Where necessary to support device-discovery functionality, information about nearby devices detected on the local network may be transmitted to a third-party service provider acting on LG’s behalf to identify compatible devices.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Roku TVs may detect other devices on the home network to support features like AirPlay, as described in our privacy policy.

Samsung:

No. Samsung TVs do not scan your home Wi-Fi network to collect or transmit an inventory of other connected devices. The TV only communicates with compatible devices that customers actively choose to connect (such as for casting or via the SmartThings app under their Samsung Account) to provide smart home control, not to monitor other devices on your network.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

Users may connect their TCL Smart TV to other devices so they can control those devices. For some on-device functions, such as screen casting or connecting devices to each other, the TV may detect other devices on the same Wi-Fi network. That data is normally exchanged only between the devices. If a connection problem occurs, diagnostics may report the name of the device involved. When a consumer chooses to control the TV through a voice service such as Amazon Alexa, data is exchanged between the TV, TCL’s cloud, and Amazon so the service can function.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

11. Can users entirely opt out of transmitting all forms of data?

Amazon:

No. Basic functionality like downloading apps and streaming content requires transmitting data. However, Fire TV does provide customers the ability to control the collection or transmission of certain data, including data about the frequency and duration of use of third-party apps and about what customers have watched in third-party apps.

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

Users cannot opt out of 100% of data transmission while connected to the internet. Essential system telemetry (device model, OS version, activation status, security updates) is mandatory for basic operation.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

Users can stop the transmission of personal data associated with smart TV services by withdrawing their acceptance of the Privacy Policy or Terms of Use. If they do so, smart TV services will no longer be available, and the data transmission required to provide those services will cease. The TV can still be used for basic functions that do not require smart TV services, such as Live TV or HDMI inputs.

Users can also separately choose whether to use optional features such as voice recognition, ACR, and interest-based advertising. These features require separate agreements and can be reviewed, managed, or withdrawn through the TV settings at any time. Declining or withdrawing these optional agreements does not prevent users from using core smart TV functionality.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

No, but Roku offers privacy settings for voice data, Smart TV Experience, and ad personalization.

Samsung:

No, not all forms. At minimum, data is needed to run a digital platform (e.g. to provide the service and security).

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

Some data is transmitted to TCL because the Smart TV services and functions the user chooses depend on such data. Users can opt out of sending TCL the limited interaction data collected for diagnostics and product improvement.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

12. Are users automatically opted out by default when setting up the TV?

Amazon:

Customers are not opted out of all data transmission by default. Again, basic device functionality requires data to be transmitted. However, there are some Fire TV features like Automatic Content Recognition that are default off and that customers must affirmatively turn on in order to allow those features to work and transmit data.

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

During initial setup, options such as Usage & Diagnostics sharing, personalized recommendations/ads, and Google Account Web & App Activity tracking are enabled by default unless opted out.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

Yes. Users can choose to opt-in by accepting each applicable agreement before the relevant services or features are enabled. Optional features such as voice recognition, ACR, and interest-based advertising are not enabled by default . Users can also manage or withdraw their consent through the TV settings at any time.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Smart TV Experience is off by default in the US.

Samsung:

Yes. For Viewing Information Services (VIS), which includes Automatic Content Recognition (ACR), consumers are opted out by default and must affirmatively enable it.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

Users can opt out of sending TCL the limited interaction data collected for diagnostics and product improvement.

The ACR technology on those TCL Smart TVs which support that feature comes from the operating system provider or third-party software providers. Users choose whether to turn on ACR when they first set up the TV, and they can turn it off at any time in the ACR provider’s privacy settings. Before ACR is turned on, the user must agree to the ACR provider’s terms and conditions. Those terms and privacy policies explain what viewing data the provider may store or transmit with the user’s consent.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

13. If users opt out, does the TV store any of these forms of data internally for potential use at a later date?

Amazon:

No. If a customer has opted out of Fire TV collecting data, that data will not be collected unless the customer re-enables collection.

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

If cloud tracking is disabled, local temporary caches and system operational buffers remain on-device for immediate system execution and local performance before deletion.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

No. If a user withdraws consent under an applicable agreement, data previously collected under that agreement is handled in accordance with LG’s applicable data retention and deletion policies, including deletion or anonymization where appropriate, and is not retained for potential future use.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Roku’s ad personalization setting affects which ads users see. Data is still collected and used for other purposes, as described in our privacy policy.

Samsung:

No. If users opt out, the TV stops collecting new viewing data immediately and does not store it internally for later use. Once you disable the Viewing Information Services (VIS), any previously collected ACR data is deleted from our servers and can no longer be associated with your device.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

TCL did not provide a direct answer to this question.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

14. Does disconnecting a TV from the internet prevent all these forms of data transmission?

Amazon:

Yes.

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

Severing internet access (disconnecting Wi-Fi or removing Ethernet) halts all outbound external data transmission to Google cloud servers. Of course this also stops any streaming service from operating.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

Yes. A TV must be connected to the internet to transmit data. For voice recognition specifically, voice data is not stored for later upload when the TV is offline and is not transmitted when the connection is restored.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Data can’t reach Roku’s servers without an internet connection.

Samsung:

Yes. A TV without internet access cannot transmit data to Samsung. Bluetooth is used only for local connections the customer sets up, such as remotes, headphones, or soundbars, and is not used to transmit viewing or advertising data. Samsung TVs do not connect to open Wi-Fi networks on their own.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

Disconnecting a TCL TV from the internet stops data from being sent to remote servers.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

15. If users disconnect a TV from the internet, does the TV store any of these forms of data internally for potential use at a later date?

Amazon:

Yes, smart TVs will store some data locally to transmit once connectivity has been re-established. For example, if an application were to crash while your smart TV was offline, the device might store that data locally to be able to transmit it once connectivity has been reestablished—for the purpose of ensuring your devices and services are working as they should.

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

Android-level system event logs and diagnostic buffers are stored locally on-device and may sync or transmit crash/error reports once an internet connection is restored.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

No. If the TV is disconnected from the internet, it does not store this information internally for later transmission or use when the internet connection is restored. For example, voice recognition data is not stored for later upload while the TV is offline and is not subsequently transmitted when the internet connection is restored.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Samsung:

Yes, but is dependent upon what features are enabled on the TV and the model year of the device.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

Unless a consumer has opted out, the TV stores certain diagnostic and performance data while offline, which is processed once the TV reconnects.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

16. Is collected data encrypted on device? Is it encrypted in transit? Is it encrypted end-to-end?

Amazon:

Data is encrypted in transit.

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

On-device: YES (Android file-based encryption). In transit: YES (TLS/HTTPS). End-to-end: NO for standard queries/telemetry, as Google servers must decrypt requests to process voice commands and content recommendations.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

Personal information, such as LG Account information, is encrypted. Other information, such as STT results, may be stored without encryption. All data transmitted from the device to the server is sent through an encrypted channel.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Roku uses industry-standard security measures to protect data, specifically end-to-end encryption.

Samsung:

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

Data collected by TCL is encrypted in transit.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

17. Can users erase data that has already been collected by your company and its partners?

Yes. Customers have a variety of ways to easily manage data Amazon collects, including deletion options.

Apple:

At Apple, we respect users’ ability to know, access, correct, transfer, restrict the processing of, and delete their personal data. Users worldwide can delete data associated with their account at the Apple Data and Privacy page at privacy.apple.com.

Google:

Users can review, manage, and permanently delete their activity history, voice recordings, and personalized search data via the Google My Activity portal (myactivity.google.com).

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

Users can request deletion of their personal information by contacting LG via the email address provided in the Privacy Policy. They also can request deletion of certain data—including voice information and viewing information—directly through the TV’s settings.

When a user withdraws consent or requests deletion, LG deletes the relevant data in accordance with its data retention and deletion policies.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Users can submit a deletion request at privacy.roku.com, and we process it in accordance with applicable law.

Samsung:

Yes, customers may request to have their data deleted. Customers may also reset their device advertising ID, which means previous Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) data can no longer be associated with their device.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

Users can ask TCL to delete data it has collected through TCL’s official privacy request channels.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

John Higgins
excerpt:
Every TV company is spying on you, not just LG. Like other tech companies, they collect lots of information, and while some is necessary for products to work, not all of it is — and could include details you’d prefer to keep private. Many customers are concerned about how TVs and streaming devices might be spying: listening to what you say, taking screenshots of everything you watch, storing sensitive information on your TV, and sharing your data with the cloud.

To find out what TV and streaming device companies are doing, I decided to ask every one to explain itself. I put together 17 yes-or-no questions, like “Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?” so that companies couldn’t just link to a confusing and legalese-ridden privacy policy. TV users deserve to know the answers.

title: Google Fi brings back network switching with ‘secondary’ partner, expands W+ beyond Pixel
snippet: Google Fi Wireless is rolling out a big update today with the return of network switching thanks to a “secondary” partner. more…
fullText:
Google Fi Wireless is rolling out a big update today with the return of network switching thanks to a “secondary” partner.

At the beginning, Project Fi was known for giving subscribers access to both T-Mobile and Sprint networks. Over time, the second partner went away, leaving one predominant network.

Google Fi is now bringing back a second partner as part of its new “super network.” Most users will be on the “Primary network,” but Google Fi will automatically switch users to the “Secondary network” if it meaningfully improves performance with so-called “smart thresholds” for doing so. At launch, there is no manual switching.

Google is not naming the second network today, but did share that Ultra Wideband is supported. Officially, you are switching between “two of America’s fastest 5G networks.”

	

Fi Wireless does note that users have top priority, so data is never deprioritized on the Primary network. Meanwhile, there’s “highest QCI priority” on the backup network that means subscribers are among the last to be slowed down when there’s congestion. This is also available internationally when local partner networks are available with the Flexible and Unlimited Premium plans.

Network switching will first be supported on Pixel 9 and newer devices that have a Google Fi eSIM (and no other SIM active). It makes use of Android’s Multiple Enabled Profiles (MEP) eSIM technology that allows for two carrier profiles on a single chip.

	

The Google Fi app gains a “Your super network” card in the Home tab that shows whether you’re connected to the Primary or Secondary network. “See activity” lets you view switching history and when it last occurred. Google will also note if you’re in range of W+ networks.

Google today is also expanding its Wi-Fi Auto Connect+ network beyond Pixel phones to select Samsung Galaxy (S23, Fold/Flip 5, and newer) and modern Motorola phones. These premium Wi-Fi networks are available in millions of airports, malls, stores, and restaurants. The connection happens automatically, with the Google Fi Virtual Carrier Network encrypting data. 

The final update today sees the companion app gain “Ask Fi.” This AI-powered chat is meant to quickly provide answers and guided troubleshooting for common issues. You can request human support with seamless handoff that keeps the chat context.

These Google Fi updates start rolling out today, with network switching seeing gradual availability. This launch is accompanied by several deals:

“For new subscribers, get $500 off instantly and $599 back over 24 monthly credits when you purchase the new Google Pixel 11 Pro, plus $10/mo service credit for 2 years with the Unlimited Premium plan. Ends 11/18/26.”

“Already have a Pixel but not using Google Fi? Get 50% off select unlimited plans for 12 months. Ends 12/1/26.”

title: Samsung’s next cheap phone will have a much bigger battery than the Galaxy S26 Ultra
snippet: According to a new report, Samsung’s upcoming mid-range smartphone is getting a big battery upgrade that outdoes that company’s current $1,400 flagship. more…
fullText:
According to a new report, Samsung’s upcoming mid-range smartphone is getting a big battery upgrade that outdoes that company’s current $1,400 flagship.

GalaxyClub reports that the Samsung Galaxy A38 will ship with a 6,000 mAh battery. That’s a 20% jump over Samsung’s typical 5,000 mAh batteries that have been in Galaxy A series phones for the past few years, and is also a 20% jump from the company’s current flagship Galaxy S26 Ultra.

Compared to the likes of many other Android phones on the international market, 6,000 mAh isn’t huge. Honor, for example, launched new phones with 10,000 mAh batteries just a couple of weeks ago. But in the context of Samsung, this is a welcome step forward. The company finally embraced silicon-carbon in its latest foldables and, while it’s unclear if that’s what we’re seeing here, it’s very obvious that Samsung is making a push to increase its battery capacity moving forward.

Based on the Galaxy A37’s launch date, the Galaxy A38 is likely to make its debut in early 2027.

	

Galaxy S27 is rumored to make some minor battery upgrades as well.

title: Apple TV launches new sign language accessibility feature
snippet: Apple today launched a neat new accessibility feature for the Apple TV streaming service. Users will now have the option to watch with a sign language interpretation for some of Apple’s original movies. The feature is launching this Friday with the debut of the new film Being Heumann, as well as F1: The Movie. Support for more titles will follow later. more…
fullText:
Apple today launched a neat new accessibility feature for the Apple TV streaming service. Users will now have the option to watch with a sign language interpretation for some of Apple’s original movies. 

The feature is launching this Friday with the debut of the new film Being Heumann, as well as F1: The Movie. Support for more titles will follow later.

Alongside those two films, Apple said that sign language options will be available for Greyhound and Way of the Warrior Kid later this year, with more to come.

To access the new functionality, you need to be using the Apple TV app on iPhone, iPad or Mac running 27.2 or later. The feature will also be available on some versions of the Apple TV app on other platforms. 

By default, the Sign Language controls are hidden. If you want to use the feature, firstly go to the Settings app -> TV app, and enable the Sign Language display. 

Then, on eligible titles, a new Sign Language button will appear in the player controls. You can simply toggle to enable, and choose from American Sign Language or British Sign Language modes. 

When enabled, a signing interpreter then appears in the corner of the frame, synced with the video playback. 

When browsing the catalog, sign language availability will also be shown next to the usual subtitle and audio language information. Users will also be able to search “with ASL” or “with BSL” to find compatible titles.

title: Motorola Signature 27 gets Pixel’s Gemini Intelligence features with Rambler, Create My Widget
snippet: Motorola is adopting Google’s Gemini Intelligence features in the first major expansion beyond Pixel, with Gboard’s Rambler and more supported. more…
fullText:
Motorola is adopting Google’s Gemini Intelligence features in the first major expansion beyond Pixel, with Gboard’s Rambler and more supported.

Motorola Signature 27 goes official with true flagship specs and a $1,599 price tag

While Google’s Gemini Intelligence is technically supporting Samusng’s latest Galaxy devices too, it’s Motorola that’s opening the floodgates beyond the Pixel lineup. The new Motorola Signature 27 is officially getting support for the bulk of Google’s new features, including “Create My Widget” which, so far, has only been available on Googlebook.

Supported Gemini Intelligence features on Motorola Signature 27 include:

Create My Widget

Gboard Rambler

Gboard Sign-to-Text

Gemini task automation

Taking those one by one, “Create My Widget” is, again, the most intriguing addition. Google announced this feature early this year but, even for Google Pixel phones, it’s not yet gone live. That’s presumably soon to change, seeing as Motorola’s launch date for this device is November 19 and the company confirmed that this will be available out of the box on that date.

	

Regardless, the feature itself allows users to describe the functionality they want in a widget to Gemini before the AI spits out a functional widget.

	

Gboard Rambler and Sign-to-Text are also supported here. The former supports taking long-winded voice-to-text prompts and cleaning up filler words and even add formatting, while Sign-to-Text translates American Sign Language via video to English text.

Finally, Gemini task automation allows users to assign certain tasks to Gemini, with the AI then running the bulk of the task through supported apps such as Uber and DoorDash in the background. This is also available on Pixel and select Samsung Galaxy devices.

Motorola Signature 27 pre-orders are open now, with the flagship priced at $1,599 in the US.

fullText:
A cozy habit tracker, a smarter snippet library, and a rooster that wants you out of bed: this year’s Shipaton winners offer plenty of new apps to explore.

RevenueCat’s annual app-building competition drew 3,985 project submissions in 2026, according to its winner announcement. Across the 20 first-place categories, developers tackled everyday frustrations, built inventive games, and found new ways to connect people.

Here’s a look at every first-place winner:

Read RevenueCat’s full winner announcement

	

Mio turns everyday habits into a cozy game

1st place • Grand Prize Winner

Keeping a routine is easier when there’s something to look forward to. Mio pairs self-care and habit tracking with a pixel companion that grows as you make progress. Check off habits, earn coins, and unlock new companions and collectibles, with friends and groups adding a social reason to keep going.

Mio took Shipaton’s Grand Prize, with RevenueCat highlighting its revenue and growth in a crowded habit-tracking market.

Boop makes every dog walk a collecting adventure

1st place • #BuildInPublic

That dog you met on your morning walk can become part of your collection. Boop identifies cats and dogs and turns their photos into stickers for a digital book, giving pet lovers a playful reason to pay attention to the animals around them.

Creator Taiwo Omisore’s “100 Boops” challenge took the app into the real world, where printed pet portraits and conversations with owners helped shape the product. That hands-on approach earned Boop first place in #BuildInPublic.

Nitelore puts neon racing in your pocket

1st place • Grand Prize Winner

If you have fond memories of futuristic arcade racers, Nitelore has a familiar appeal: hovering vehicles, neon tracks, and plenty of speed. Chase your own ghost in time trials, take on combat races, or compete online.

Free tracks offer a starting point, while paid unlocks and daily and weekly challenges give players more to explore. RevenueCat’s Best Game judges singled out the art direction, effects, and haptics.

See as Me makes color blindness easier to understand

1st place • RevenueCat Peace Prize

Explaining how you see color can be surprisingly difficult. See as Me: Colorblind makes that conversation visual, using a split-screen camera to compare different types and degrees of color blindness. A shareable link lets someone else see the comparison without installing the app.

Developer Javier Jiménez drew on his own experience with protanopia. That personal perspective helped the app earn the RevenueCat Peace Prize.

Clucky gives your alarm clock a personality

1st place • RevenueCat Design Award

Clucky’s rooster is determined to get you out of bed. Turning off an alarm can require solving a problem, moving around, or finding an object, bringing a little friction to the temptation to snooze.

Its personality runs through the entire interface, including a time picker that uses the rooster’s scrolling eyes and yellow beak. That consistent character, animation, and attention to detail earned Clucky the RevenueCat Design Award.

Adversary adds a twist to the memory game

1st place • Grand Prize Winner

Adversary starts with a familiar challenge: flip cards and find matching pairs. The catch is a hidden Danger card with no matching partner. Reveal it, and an ad becomes part of the board you’re trying to remember.

That idea earned Niv Ben-porath’s game the Catvertising Award. Players can continue with ads after an initial ad-free period, or choose a permanent unlock that removes ads and adds difficulty options.

Bubble Games brings everyone’s phones together

1st place • Next Gen Award

Put a few phones on the table, and Bubble Games turns their screens into a shared game board. Objects move between devices as friends compete in minigames, including a virtual hot potato.

Built by four software engineering students at Université Laval, the Next Gen Award winner uses the phones people already have to create a shared activity. Its Shipaton submission includes ten minigames. The winner announcement links to the Android release on Google Play.

GRIDLOCK gives tic-tac-toe room to grow

1st place • HAMM Award (Help Apps Make Money)

GRIDLOCK takes a game everyone knows and adds up to four players, online rooms, and eleven special moves. The result offers more ways to disrupt an opponent’s plans than the familiar three-by-three board.

Its HAMM Award win recognizes how the business model fits the game: a shared Credits currency connects rewarded ads, optional packs, and a subscription, while core modes remain free. Players can choose the option that fits how often they play.

Just Add starts dinner with what you want to eat

1st place • Influencer Award – Nutrition & Healthy Eating: Abbey’s Kitchen

Just Add begins with a craving. Type what you feel like eating, describe it aloud, or take a photo, and the app suggests three meals built around it, adding protein, fiber, and healthy fats to round out the plate.

Shopping support, hands-free cooking, and remembered preferences help carry the idea through to dinner. The winner of Abbey’s Kitchen’s nutrition challenge also impressed judges with a dinner-host feature that accounts for other people’s preferences.

SnipStash keeps reusable content close at hand

1st place • Influencer Award – Productivity: Christopher Lawley

The reply you send every week, the PDF you keep hunting for, and the image you paste repeatedly can all live in SnipStash. It organizes reusable text, images, and files across iPhone, iPad, and Mac, with a keyboard, Mac quick palette, hotkeys, and Shortcuts bringing them within reach.

Private iCloud sync connects the library across devices. Its speed and native interface helped it win Christopher Lawley’s productivity challenge.

Rehearse helps you practice the difficult conversation

1st place • Influencer Award – Career Coaching: Leadership Heather

Knowing what you want to say and saying it aloud are different things. Rehearse – Hard Conversations gives you an AI counterpart to practice with before a difficult workplace discussion.

Choose from 33 prepared scenarios or bring your own situation, then review feedback on clarity, empathy, assertiveness, and structure. A prep card helps you take the useful points into the real conversation. The app won Leadership Heather’s career-coaching challenge for its focused, straightforward approach.

Game Magnet saves the game you spotted in a video

1st place • Influencer Award – Gaming: Mr Lewis Blogs Gaming

You see a game in a short video, mean to look it up later, and forget its name. Game Magnet lets you share the clip to identify the games and save them to your backlog.

Processing happens in the background, with a notification when the result is ready. Shelves, ratings, and ranked lists help organize what comes next. The app won Mr Lewis Blogs Gaming’s challenge by making discovery and keeping track of games easier.

FeelGood offers movement that fits your day

1st place • Influencer Award – Yoga & Fitness: Simone Sharice

FeelGood: Movement Menu starts with a short check-in about your energy, available time, and how you want to feel. It then offers a small menu of movement, with an appetizer, main, and optional sides.

The options span yoga, Pilates, strength, walking, stretching, and breathing. Rest is part of the experience, too. Yusra Salam and Ameena Malik’s app won Simone Sharice’s yoga and fitness challenge, with judges praising its calm, inviting design.

BoatBrawl gets friends into the same battle

1st place • Ship Kotlin Everywhere

BoatBrawl brings arcade boat battles to a group of up to eight players. Steer, fire, and scramble through interactive arenas, with bots and shared-screen play offering more ways to join in.

Rehaan Cubes and Ashwin K M used Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform to bring the game across phones and computers, including iOS, Android, Mac, Windows, and the web. Its smooth browser play helped it take JetBrains’ Ship Kotlin Everywhere award.

Trazo gives golf videos a broadcast-style finish

1st place • Most Viral App

Trazo: Golf Ball Tracer adds a ball-flight line to your own golf videos. Select the ball twice to start, and the processing runs on the phone.

Julian Praest’s app won Most Viral App for the way its team introduced the product through organic content. Golf humor and practical advice set up the tracer reveal, making the finished video part of the pitch. For golfers, the appeal is simple: make the shot easier to follow when you share it.

Grandfolio helps collectors identify their next find

1st place • Best App for Galaxy

One Piece Card Game collectors know that similar-looking cards can be very different finds. Grandfolio helps identify artwork variants, manage duplicates, and track collection prices and progress.

The Best App for Galaxy winner impressed judges with layouts that adapt to folded, tabletop, and open-screen use. There’s an App Store release for Apple users, too, making this a relevant discovery even if your collection starts on an iPhone.

Let’s Get Support focuses on the people giving support

1st place • Replit’s Idea to Income

Let’s Get Support by 3Dadz is designed for partners, parents, and friends affected by someone else’s addiction. Check-ins, journaling, boundary-setting tools, and local resources give those supporters a place to focus on their own needs.

Joshua Burgess and Aaryn B. built the app from community conversations in British Columbia, using Replit to turn the idea into a live product. It won Replit’s Idea to Income award. The announcement links to its Android release.

PoquitoTalk helps everyday conversations cross languages

1st place • The Growth Loop Award

PoquitoTalk: Bocas del Toro turns English into local Spanish voice notes for WhatsApp and helps translate the replies. The recipient doesn’t need to install the app, keeping the conversation in a tool people already use.

Creator Dorien Van den Abbeele drew on years of life in Bocas del Toro. Its Growth Loop Award recognizes extensive growth experiments and an honest account of what the measurements could show. The announcement links to Google Play.

Parky! puts useful park updates on your Lock Screen

1st place • Keep Them Coming Back Award

Parky! combines wait times, dining availability, and memories from Disney and Universal visits. Built by former Disney Cast Member Chase Van Derrick, it aims to offer useful help throughout a park day.

Dining alerts can become conversations on the Lock Screen, where you can ask about another time or restaurant. Alongside queue Live Activities and recap messages, those interactive notifications helped Parky! win the Keep Them Coming Back Award.

In Your Own Words makes room for a minute of practice

1st place • Funnel Vision Award

In Your Own Words offers short, real-world speaking scenarios and feedback on pace, hesitation, and filler words. Speech analysis takes place on the phone, giving users a way to practice the words before they need them.

Natasha Wilson’s app won the Funnel Vision Award for connecting a web quiz, a relevant practice deck, and a web purchase that unlocks access in the app. The introduction to the product begins before the download.

Winner • Conflict of Interest Award

Friendpire turns the idea of a board-game night with friends into a shared hex-tile world. Gather resources, build farms and docks, and grow an empire together. RevenueCat employee Erik MacInnis built the game to make it easier to stay connected with friends who rarely find time to play.

Friendpire won the separate Conflict of Interest Award, which was open to RevenueCat and sponsor employees and judged by Shipaton participants. It is included here as an optional sidebar and is not part of the 20 first-place count above.

Discover your next app

From a useful tool for the workday to a game for your next night in, Shipaton’s winners show how much can come from taking an idea all the way to a shipped app. Explore the winners above, or browse RevenueCat’s full announcement for more apps from the competition.

title: Google’s AI search fumbles leave schools in the lurch
snippet: Good morning, and happy Ocarina of Time day to all who celebrate. Oh, and speaking of celebrating: congratulations to the real winners of the midterms, YouTube and Twitch streamers. Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe. more…
fullText:
Good morning, and happy Ocarina of Time day to all who celebrate. Oh, and speaking of celebrating: congratulations to the real winners of the midterms, YouTube and Twitch streamers.

Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

It’s hard to overstate how reliant US school districts are on Google. Almost every school board in the country purchases Chromebooks for their students, many of whom are able to take them home and treat them as personal laptops. IT and procurement managers like them because they’re relatively cheap and offer zero-touch enrollment, which lowers upfront and ongoing maintenance costs. Teachers also like them because Google Classroom is relatively intuitive and ChromeOS is optimized for most other web-based education platforms.

	

But this reliance on Google’s tech stack comes at a cost: school boards are forced to comply with the company’s capricious terms of service, in particular when it comes to the creeping proliferation of AI across its products. 

Things came to a head earlier this week when the New York Times reported that changes to the Google Search experience in schools will require opting into Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and, perhaps most importantly, AI Overviews. The move actually comes after Google was pressured to make student AI usage opt-in. Google’s justification: search and AI are now “deeply integrated” in the tech stack, so disabling one means disabling the other.

Google’s alternative to AI Overviews is a new Guided Learning feature, which replaces search’s primary function — solving a problem — with a step-by-step guide that helps a student understand said problem.

Former FTC Chair Lina Khan took to X to decry the move: “Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI,” she said. “This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service. Multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains unchastened. As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”

I have a feeling Google will need to walk back this decision in some form. As 9to5’s Ben Schoon points out, it’s comically easy to disable AI Overviews in the current version of Google Search, and it doesn’t seem to have a detrimental impact on the subsequent results. But Google is likely worried that if it is forced to carve out versions of the search experience for specific user bases, revenue from its burgeoning AI Overviews ad business may be impacted.

Even if Google sticks to its proverbial guns, the move exposes a rift between the public, particularly parents, and the tech giants pushing AI on their users. Furthermore, the AI boom has had a direct impact on educators’ ability to purchase new hardware and upgrade old Chromebook fleets, since component prices have increased by as much as 5x over the past year. Some lower-income districts are even recalling Chromebooks from students, reverting to a shared laptop pool to save money.

✉️ Inbox

Redmagic 12 Pro review: You’ve never gamed on a phone like this before. We talked about this phone on The Sideload this week: as Android gets better for games, I think gaming phones will be increasingly important for Android.

The Sideload 050: The phones Samsung and Google won’t make

Google has fixed Android Auto issues on Samsung Galaxy phones running One UI 9 [U]

Google confirms Android’s new ‘Family Hub’ feature, and this is what it looks like. Android is getting a bit more family-friendly.

Xiaomi confirms Android 17 HyperOS 4 rollout schedule for these devices

Galaxy Z Fold 8 sales spike amid iPhone Duo release and ‘crackgate’ debacle. The iPhone Duo’s display issues may not yet constitute a scandal, but Samsung’s category lead has never seemed so assured.

Google confirms something was draining Pixel Watch batteries, fix rolling out. Pixel owners seemingly can’t catch a break.

Android Auto 18.1 update rolling out with additional prep for light mode and redesign. Another minor redesign is coming to what is arguably the best version of Android out there.

Google’s Stadia Controller dream lives on in the $50 Xbox Nano Controller. I need this little guy.

‘Cyclon’ uses an old Google Pixel to let AI do literally everything for you – who wants this? Nobody, Ben. Nobody.

ChatGPT has hit roughly 20% of Google Search volume, OpenAI says. This is a staggering number achieved in only four years. It’s no wonder Google is freaking out.

Peak Design’s new wireless charging stand pulls double duty, literally. I saw prototypes for these way back at CES in January, and the final versions look way more polished. Looking forward to trying them.

Google Messages redesigning pinned chats and moving search

Google Photos now lets you turn off background music in Memories. Thank goodness. I genuinely hate this feature.

Google will fix Nest devices that didn’t adjust for Daylight Savings, breaking alarms and more. Oh, Canada.

Microsoft says it now sucks less to use a Windows PC with 8GB of RAM. Seems like Google isn’t the only company doubling down on efficiency.

Three months in, Galaxy Z Fold 8’s cameras aren’t enough, and Fold 9 might not fix it. Ben’s absolutely right about this: I love my Fold 8, but its cameras are straight-up terrible.

The first Snapdragon phone with Android Linux Terminal support is here

Nothing teases screen-less product launching next month, ‘couldn’t have been an app’. This certainly sounds like something that records your every interaction. Couldn’t Bee, right?

‘Enough Phone’ is an Android phone roughly the size of iPhone 13 Mini, launching in 2027. I have to respect the gumption of releasing a phone that will almost certainly be a one-off, but is this what people are really after in 2027?

Henry Cavill builds 16-bit ‘Mustache Protocol’ game on Googlebook for a good cause. This is not doing the Googlebook brand any favors.

➡️ FWD:

For a much less complicated relationship with Google Search, try its Ocarina of Time Easter egg. Search for “Zelda” or “Ocarina of Time,” then tap the Master Sword to travel back to a 1998-style results page, complete with Link’s sound effects. It’s a trip down memory lane to a time when, as even Google acknowledges, things were a whole lot simpler.

Was AI on the ballot? According to Ben Thompson at Stratechery, it was in a big way. Democrats and Republicans both rejected data centers, but Democrats want to actually pass some regulation reining in the hyperscalers’ and frontier labs’ ambitions.

First we were short on compute, but that ramped; now we are short on memory, but that will ramp; we were coming close to being short on power, but that will be rectified. The final constraint is political, and that may be the most imposing constraint of all. Not only is it harder to solve, but it actually interferes with solving the other constraints. Many of the theories about AI assume that it becomes a commodity; I think it’s just as likely we are looking at scarcity for much longer than we expected, which will have ripple effects on everything.

Is it possible to pass broad AI regulation that will slow down an industry that has been allowed to run unchecked since Trump’s reelection in 2024? And is it in the best interest of these companies to support it, even if it means a short-term slowdown at a time when the two biggest AI labs, Anthropic and OpenAI, are about to IPO?

Some fascinating developments in the $6.3 billion Binance hack: turns out it was yet another case of social engineering. A Binance engineer was lured into a fake job interview, before which he downloaded malware that let hackers breach his computer and, eventually, others on the network.

🗑️ Trash

After my discussion with Will last week about the death of browsers, it came as no surprise to learn that Brave is being sued by the New York Times for copyright infringement. Brave is accused of scraping paywalled material from sites like nytimes.com and selling access to it through a search API to AI companies, which use it as training data. Yes, it’s difficult to earn money as a browser maker (see Arc for another compelling example), but this is particularly egregious, even for a company familiar with shady business practices.

Like what you just read? Subscribe to Inbox today and get it in your email every Tuesday and Thursday morning. Got feedback? Send us an email.

You can also support us by becoming a 9to5Google Pro member, starting at just $5/month. You get bonus podcast episodes, access to our members-only Discord server, and lots more.

Thanks for reading, and have a great day. I’ll talk to you on Tuesday.

—Daniel

title: Google Fi’s ‘Super Network’ Hops Networks to Keep Your Pixel Phone Connected
snippet: Automatic network switching for Pixel phones could mean fewer mobile dead zones.
fullText:
Even in areas that seem abundant with overlapping cellular coverage, phones sometimes sputter when you’re looking up information or trying to get directions when your carrier’s signal gets weak. To avoid those annoying interruptions, Google Fi Wireless is rolling out what it’s calling a “super network” feature. It automatically switches your phone between two 5G networks to maintain the best connection.

The new capability works only on Google’s phones, starting with the Pixel 9 and newer Pixel models.

The super network is included free for existing Google Fi customers on all of its plans: Flexible, Unlimited Essentials, Unlimited Standard and Unlimited Premium.

			

More from CNET

Google says that it’s using “two top 5G networks,” but the company is refusing to reveal which networks those are in the US. Traditionally Google Fi runs on T-Mobile’s network.

The network switching also applies when you’re traveling internationally, and is included in the Unlimited Premium and Flexible plans.

According to a source at Google, the phone will use two eSIM slots to switch between networks, but it will appear to only use a single eSIM on the customer’s phone. A fine-print disclaimer notes that any other eSIMs on your device must be disabled, which is worth knowing for anyone that already uses multiple carriers on a single device.

In addition to the super network news, Google said its Wi-Fi Auto Connect Plus feature is available in millions of more locations across the US. If the phone is in an area where cellular is spotty and a compatible Wi-Fi network is nearby, it automatically makes an encrypted connection if the Wi-Fi network is stronger.

Wi-Fi Auto Connect Plus is available on Pixel phones, but is also becoming available on Samsung phones running One UI 9 or later and “select modern Motorola phones.”
